questions.stem: Medium sized artery is characterized by: |
questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: Medium-sized (muscular) arteries are the most numerous and widely distributed artery type in the body, forming the many named arteries supplying individual organs and regions (such as the brachial, femoral, radial, and coronary arteries), in contrast to the few large elastic arteries (aorta and its major branches) and the much smaller, more localised arterioles. Their walls are dominated by a thick tunica media built mainly of smooth muscle (with a single, well-defined internal elastic lamina and a less prominent external elastic lamina), rather than by the many concentric elastic laminae that define large elastic arteries. The exam takeaway is to associate 'muscular artery' with 'the most common, widely distributed artery type', in contrast to elastic arteries (fewer, defined by 40-70 elastic laminae) and arterioles (smallest, primary site of vascular resistance).

distractorNotes.A: It is the tunica media, not the adventitia, that is the thickest and most defining layer of a medium (muscular) artery's wall.
distractorNotes.B: The 40-70 elastic membrane feature belongs specifically to large elastic arteries (like the aorta), not medium/muscular arteries, whose media is instead dominated by smooth muscle.
distractorNotes.C: Having a continuous, non-fenestrated endothelium is a feature shared by essentially all arteries (and continuous capillaries), so it does not specifically distinguish medium arteries.

questions.stem: Blood capillaries in exocrine glands are:
questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: Exocrine glands, such as the pancreas and salivary glands, require efficient bulk movement of fluid and small solutes to support active secretion, and their capillary beds are accordingly of the fenestrated (visceral) type -- endothelium perforated by small pores, typically covered by a thin diaphragm, sitting atop a continuous basement membrane. This structural adaptation allows rapid passage of water and small molecules between blood and the secretory acinar cells without the wholesale leakiness of a sinusoidal capillary, matching the gland's high metabolic and secretory demands. The histology takeaway is to associate fenestrated capillaries generally with secretory or absorptive/filtering organs -- endocrine and exocrine glands, the gastrointestinal mucosa, and the renal glomerulus.

distractorNotes.A: Sinusoidal capillaries, with their large gaps and often discontinuous basement membrane, are instead characteristic of organs like the liver, spleen, and bone marrow, not typical exocrine gland acini.
distractorNotes.B: 'Visceral capillaries' is essentially a synonym for fenestrated capillaries in some textbooks, but is not the conventional term used to distinguish this answer from option C in this bank.
distractorNotes.D: 'Somatic capillaries' is the term used for continuous (non-fenestrated) capillaries found in muscle, skin, and the CNS, the opposite structural category from what supports active glandular secretion.

questions.stem: It is absent in Klinefelter syndrome | 9- Addition of a fragmented segment of one chromosome to the homologous chromosome is known as:
variants: [EOY 104 FINALS (answered) (1) (1).pdf p13 #0] It is absent in Klinefelter syndrome | 9- Addition of a fragmented segment of one chromosome to the homologous chromosome is known as: :: A) Duplication B) Isochromosome C) Translocation | D) Inversion
questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: Duplication is the structural chromosomal aberration in which a fragmented segment of one chromosome becomes added onto its homologous chromosome, resulting in that segment being present in an extra copy within the genome. This is structurally distinct from translocation, where a segment moves to attach to a NON-homologous chromosome rather than its own homolog, and from inversion, where a segment simply reverses its orientation within the same chromosome without any addition of material. The exam takeaway is to keep these structural aberration definitions precise: duplication adds an extra copy of a segment onto its homolog; translocation moves a segment to a different chromosome; inversion flips a segment's orientation in place.

distractorNotes.B: An isochromosome results from abnormal transverse (rather than longitudinal) division of the centromere, producing a chromosome with two identical arms, an unrelated mechanism to segment addition between homologues.
distractorNotes.C: Translocation involves a segment moving to a non-homologous chromosome, not addition of a segment to its own homologous chromosome.
distractorNotes.D: Inversion involves a segment reversing its orientation within the same chromosome, not addition of material from elsewhere.

questions.stem: Regarding the meiotic cell division (Meiosis):

options.B: Daughter cells with haploid number of chromosomes
options.D: No crossing over of chromosomes occurs | 5- The centromere in metacentric chromosome is located:

variants: [EOY 104 FINALS (answered) (1) (1).pdf p13 #4] Regarding the meiotic cell division (Meiosis): :: A) It occurs in somatic cells C) Close to the upper end D) At the terminal end of chromosome
questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: Meiosis is defined by producing daughter cells (gametes) with a haploid (n) number of chromosomes, exactly half the diploid (2n) number found in the parent germ cell, achieved through two successive divisions (meiosis I and II) that include a single round of DNA replication. This chromosome number reduction is essential for sexual reproduction, ensuring that fertilisation (fusion of two haploid gametes) restores the normal diploid chromosome number in the resulting zygote. The exam takeaway is to fix 'germ cells, two divisions, haploid daughter cells, crossing over occurs' as meiosis's defining profile, the mirror opposite of mitosis.

distractorNotes.A: Meiosis occurs specifically in germ cells, not somatic cells, which instead undergo mitosis.
distractorNotes.C: Meiosis is two successive divisions (meiosis I and II), not a single division.
distractorNotes.D: Crossing over between homologous chromosomes is a defining, essential feature of meiosis (occurring during prophase I), not something absent from it.

questions.stem: Regarding the Red pulp of the spleen: ١
questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: The red pulp of the spleen is defined by its network of venous sinusoids interspersed among the Billroth cords, together forming the specialised, slow-flow architecture that allows red blood cells to be closely screened for age or damage before returning to the circulation. This is distinct from the white pulp's central arteriole landmark and four-zone lymphoid architecture, and the spleen has no mucus glands at all, being a lymphoid/haematological organ rather than a secretory gland.

distractorNotes.A: A central arteriole is a landmark of the white pulp, not the red pulp.
distractorNotes.C: The spleen contains no mucus glands; this is not a splenic feature at all.
distractorNotes.D: The four-zone architecture (periarteriolar lymphatic sheath, germinal centre, follicular/mantle zone, marginal zone) describes the white pulp, not the red pulp.

questions.stem: Regarding the white pulp of the spleen: | a. Contains a central arteriole at one side | b. Is lined by stave cells | c. Rich in numerous RBCs | d. Formed of blood sinusoids & splenic cord | 3- The paracortex of the lymph node is characterized by:

options.A: Contains a central arteriole at one side
options.D: Formed of blood sinusoids & splenic cord | 3- The paracortex of the lymph node is characterized by:
options.E: Itis the thymus dependent zone

questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: The spleen's white pulp is defined by containing a central arteriole positioned eccentrically to one side of the lymphoid tissue surrounding it, the single most reliable anatomical landmark used to identify white pulp on a histological section. This distinguishes white pulp from red pulp, which instead is characterised by blood sinusoids and splenic (Billroth) cords, is not lined by 'stave cells' (a term describing the specialised lining cells of splenic sinusoids in the red pulp, not white pulp), and is not rich in red blood cells, since it is lymphoid tissue rather than a blood-filtering compartment.

distractorNotes.B: Stave cells line the splenic sinusoids of the RED pulp, not the white pulp.
distractorNotes.C: An abundance of red blood cells is characteristic of the red pulp, not the lymphoid-tissue-dominated white pulp.
distractorNotes.D: Blood sinusoids and splenic cords are red pulp structures; describing white pulp as formed of these confuses the two splenic compartments. Only the periarteriolar lymphatic sheath (PALS) portion of white pulp, not the whole white pulp, is specifically the thymus-dependent zone, making a whole-white-pulp claim to that effect an overgeneralisation as well.

questions.stem: Segments of DNA molecules that code for formation of specific proteins are:
variants: [EOY 104 FINALS (answered) (1) (1).pdf p13 #6] Segments of DNA molecules that code for formation of specific proteins are: :: A) Kinetochores 00117 B) Cells decrease in size C) Centromere D) Chiasmata
questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: A gene is, by definition, a segment of DNA that carries the coded instructions for the synthesis of a specific protein (or functional RNA molecule), making this the direct, foundational definition being tested here. This is distinct from the kinetochore (a protein complex assembled at the centromere for spindle fibre attachment), the centromere (the constricted chromosomal region where sister chromatids are joined and where the kinetochore assembles), and chiasmata (the visible points of crossing over between homologous chromosomes during meiosis) -- all of which are structural or mechanical features of chromosomes involved in cell division, not the coding units of heredity themselves.

distractorNotes.A: Kinetochores are protein structures at the centromere serving as spindle fibre attachment sites during cell division, not DNA segments coding for proteins.
distractorNotes.C: The centromere is the chromosomal region joining sister chromatids and anchoring the kinetochore, a structural feature rather than a protein-coding DNA segment.
distractorNotes.D: Chiasmata are the visible crossover points between homologous chromosomes during meiotic prophase I, not protein-coding DNA segments.

questions.stem: Tunica adventitia with longitudinal smooth muscle fibers is seen in:
questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: The inferior vena cava is a specific, classically cited example of a large vein whose tunica adventitia contains longitudinal bundles of smooth muscle, an unusual feature for a vein and a detail commonly used in histology teaching to help identify this particular vessel on a slide. This differs from most veins, whose adventitia typically contains connective tissue with only occasional smooth muscle, making the IVC's well-developed longitudinal muscle bundles a distinguishing, named-vessel feature rather than a generic venous characteristic. The exam takeaway is to treat 'longitudinal smooth muscle in the adventitia' as a specific identifying feature of the inferior vena cava among the venous vessels tested in this bank.

distractorNotes.A: Longitudinal smooth muscle in the tunica adventitia is also a recognised secondary feature of large elastic arteries like the aorta, but in the context of this vein-focused question set, the inferior vena cava is the specific vessel this feature is being tested for.
distractorNotes.B: Medium-sized arteries are defined by their smooth-muscle-rich tunica media and prominent internal elastic lamina, not by longitudinal smooth muscle in the adventitia.
distractorNotes.C: Medium-sized veins do not have this specific, well-developed longitudinal adventitial smooth muscle feature to the extent the inferior vena cava does.

questions.stem: Two discs of protein located at centromere for spindle fibers attachment in | ١ cell division are called: |
questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: Kinetochores are the paired protein disc structures assembled on either side of the centromere, serving as the specific attachment sites for spindle fibre (kinetochore microtubule) binding during mitosis and meiosis, which is precisely the function this question describes. Each sister chromatid has its own kinetochore, allowing the two spindle poles to attach to opposite chromatids and subsequently pull them apart during anaphase. This is distinct from telomeres (protective caps at chromosome ends, unrelated to spindle attachment), genes (protein-coding DNA segments), and chiasmata (crossover points in meiosis).

distractorNotes.B: Telomeres are the protective structures capping the ends of chromosomes, preventing degradation and fusion, entirely unrelated to spindle fibre attachment.
distractorNotes.C: Genes are DNA segments coding for proteins, not the protein structures responsible for spindle fibre attachment.
distractorNotes.D: Chiasmata are the visible crossover points between homologous chromosomes during meiotic prophase I, unrelated to spindle fibre attachment at the centromere.

editorialExplanation.explanation: Pulmonary arteries are the well-known exception to the general rule that arteries carry oxygenated blood: they carry deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs specifically so it can be oxygenated there, with the now-oxygenated blood returning to the heart via the pulmonary veins -- making the claim that 'pulmonary arteries carry oxygenated blood for the lung' clearly and confidently wrong. This exception (alongside the umbilical vessels in the fetus) is one of the most frequently tested 'trick' facts in cardiovascular and respiratory anatomy precisely because it inverts the usual artery/vein oxygenation rule. The takeaway is to always treat 'artery = oxygenated, vein = deoxygenated' as a systemic-circulation rule only, with the pulmonary circulation reversed.

distractorNotes.B: True: the right phrenic nerve passes anterior to the root of the right lung as it descends toward the diaphragm, alongside the pericardiacophrenic vessels.
distractorNotes.D: True: the azygos vein arches over the root of the right lung from posterior to anterior before draining into the superior vena cava, a landmark relation on chest imaging.

questions.stem: A 17 year old boy is brought to the emergency room after an accident. He was injured and suffering from significant blood loss. Which of the following is true about his condition?

options.A: His total peripheral resistance is decreased
options.C: The firing rate of his carotid sinus nerves is increased
options.D: Sympathetic outflow to his heart and blood vessels was increased

questions.subject: Physiology

editorialExplanation.explanation: In response to significant blood loss, the fall in blood pressure reduces baroreceptor stretch and firing, which disinhibits the medullary vasomotor and cardiac centres, resulting in a marked increase in sympathetic outflow to both the heart (increasing heart rate and contractility) and the peripheral vasculature (increasing vasoconstriction and total peripheral resistance) -- the body's primary compensatory mechanism for maintaining blood pressure and perfusion despite reduced circulating volume. This is the opposite of decreased total peripheral resistance, decreased heart rate, or increased carotid sinus nerve firing, all of which would describe the situation incorrectly.

distractorNotes.A: Total peripheral resistance is INCREASED (via sympathetic vasoconstriction), not decreased, as a compensatory response to blood loss.
distractorNotes.B: Heart rate is INCREASED (compensatory tachycardia), not decreased, in response to blood loss.
distractorNotes.C: The firing rate of the carotid sinus (baroreceptor) nerves is DECREASED, not increased, as blood pressure falls and baroreceptor stretch is reduced -- this decreased firing is precisely what triggers the compensatory increase in sympathetic outflow.

questions.stem: A 49-year-old man has a pulmonary embolism that completely blocks blood flow to his left lung. As a result, which of the following will occur?

options.A: Ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) ratio in the left lung will be zero
options.B: V/Q ratio in the left lung will be lower than in the right lung
options.C: Alveolar 202 in the left lung will be approximately equal to. the PO2 in inspired air
options.D: Alveolar PO2 in the right lung will be approximately equal to the PO2 in venous blood

questions.subject: Anatomy

editorialExplanation.explanation: When perfusion (Q) to the left lung drops to zero while ventilation (V) continues, the ventilation-perfusion ratio in that lung becomes mathematically infinite (V divided by zero), not zero -- so the affected alveoli are being ventilated with fresh air but have no blood flow to exchange gas with. Under this condition, the alveolar gas composition in the unperfused lung progressively equilibrates with the composition of inspired (tracheal) air rather than being modified by blood gas exchange, since there is no perfusing blood to add carbon dioxide or remove oxygen from the alveolar space. This is the textbook 'infinite V/Q' or alveolar dead space scenario, the physiological mirror image of a shunt (zero V/Q), where perfused-but-unventilated alveoli instead equilibrate toward mixed venous blood composition.

distractorNotes.A: A V/Q ratio of zero describes the opposite extreme -- a shunt, where blood flows through unventilated alveoli -- not the zero-perfusion, normal-ventilation state described here, which instead produces an infinitely high V/Q ratio.
distractorNotes.B: The left lung's V/Q ratio in this scenario is far HIGHER than the right lung's (approaching infinity), not lower, since ventilation continues with no perfusion at all.
distractorNotes.D: The right lung, now receiving the entire cardiac output with roughly unchanged total ventilation, will have a comparatively LOW V/Q ratio and its alveolar PO2 will shift toward (but not become fully equal to) mixed venous levels -- 'approximately equal to venous blood' overstates this shift for the right lung.

questions.stem: A blood pressure of 180/120 mmHg was found in a patient aged 35. The following statements about this are true, except:

options.A: The blood pressure is elevated which will initiate reflexes that increase the cardiacoutput
options.B: Increased renin secretion could produce this finding
options.C: Increased blood level of epinephrine due to the presence of a tumor of adrenal gland
options.D: The left ventricular work is increased because of this hi gh pressure

questions.subject: Physiology

editorialExplanation.explanation: An elevated blood pressure of 180/120 mmHg would trigger the baroreceptor reflex to DECREASE, not increase, cardiac output and heart rate, as the body's negative feedback mechanism attempts to bring the elevated pressure back down toward normal -- making this statement the false one ('except') among otherwise correct facts about this scenario. The other statements are correct: increased renin secretion (activating the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system) is a genuine cause of hypertension, a catecholamine-secreting adrenal tumour (phaeochromocytoma) is a classic secondary cause of severe hypertension, and left ventricular work is genuinely increased when the heart must eject blood against this markedly elevated afterload.

distractorNotes.B: Increased renin secretion, activating the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, is a genuine, well-established mechanism that can produce hypertension.
distractorNotes.C: A catecholamine-secreting adrenal tumour (phaeochromocytoma) is a classic, well-established secondary cause of severe hypertension.
distractorNotes.D: Left ventricular work is genuinely increased at this elevated blood pressure, since the ventricle must generate more pressure (afterload) to eject blood.

questions.stem: A Child with mental retardation, hypotonia and mongol - like features has ‏ا‎ ‎performed karyotyping test. He was found to have 46 chromosomes. One 1 of the following could be seen in his karyotype: 1
questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: A child with the classic Down syndrome phenotype (mental retardation, hypotonia, mongoloid facial features) but a total chromosome count of 46 rather than the usual 47 points specifically to translocation-type Down syndrome, most commonly caused by a Robertsonian translocation between chromosomes 21 and 14 -- in this scenario, the extra chromosome 21 genetic material is fused onto chromosome 14 rather than existing as a free-standing extra chromosome, keeping the total chromosome count at 46 while still producing three functional copies of chromosome 21 material and the resulting Down syndrome phenotype. This is a key distinguishing cytogenetic finding from standard trisomy 21 (47 chromosomes) and carries different genetic counselling implications, since it can be inherited from a balanced-translocation-carrier parent. The exam takeaway is to recognise '46 chromosomes plus Down syndrome phenotype' as the signature of translocation Down syndrome, most classically involving chromosomes 21 and 14.

distractorNotes.B: The Philadelphia chromosome is associated with chronic myeloid leukaemia, an unrelated condition with no connection to the Down syndrome phenotype described.
distractorNotes.C: Duplication of chromosome 14 does not produce the Down syndrome phenotype, which is specifically linked to extra chromosome 21 material.
distractorNotes.D: Deletion of chromosome 21 would reduce, not increase, chromosome 21 gene dosage, the opposite of what causes the Down syndrome phenotype.

questions.stem: A female patient presented with mental retardation, edema of upper and lower limbs, short stature and primary amenorrhea. - . @. Her karyotype is 47 XO

options.C: Her condition is due to trisomy of sex chromosome

questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: This clinical picture -- lymphoedema of the limbs (present from birth in many cases), short stature, and primary amenorrhoea -- is the classic presentation of Turner syndrome, whose karyotype is correctly written as 45,X (informally sometimes rendered 45,XO), reflecting a total of 45 chromosomes with only a single sex chromosome present. The embedded claim of a '47,XO' karyotype is internally inconsistent, since a single-X karyotype (monosomy) should total 45 chromosomes, not 47 (which would instead suggest an extra chromosome present, contradicting the 'XO' single-X notation). The exam takeaway is to fix Turner syndrome's karyotype precisely as 45 total chromosomes with a single X and no Y, distinguishing it clearly from any XXY or trisomy karyotype.

distractorNotes.B: A patient with Turner syndrome has only ONE X chromosome, not two.
distractorNotes.C: Turner syndrome is caused by monosomy (loss) of a sex chromosome, not trisomy (gain) of one -- the opposite numerical abnormality.

questions.stem: A healthy, 45-year-old man is reading the newspaper. Which of the following muscles are used for quiet breathing?
questions.subject: Anatomy

editorialExplanation.explanation: Quiet, resting breathing is driven by the diaphragm and the external intercostal muscles, both of which are active inspiratory muscles: diaphragmatic contraction flattens the dome and increases vertical thoracic dimension, while external intercostal contraction elevates the ribs and increases the anteroposterior and transverse dimensions ('bucket-handle' and 'pump-handle' movements). Quiet expiration, by contrast, is a passive process driven by elastic recoil of the lungs and chest wall, requiring no active muscle contraction at all in a healthy person at rest. The takeaway is to reserve the internal intercostals, abdominal muscles, and sternocleidomastoid for forced/laboured breathing (active expiration and accessory inspiration respectively), not quiet resting breathing.

distractorNotes.A: Internal intercostals are expiratory (forced-expiration) muscles, not muscles used in quiet inspiration alongside the diaphragm.
distractorNotes.B: Internal intercostals and abdominal muscles are both forced-expiration muscles, not muscles active during quiet breathing at all.
distractorNotes.D: The sternocleidomastoid is an accessory inspiratory muscle recruited only during forced or laboured breathing, not during quiet breathing at rest.

Its lining epithelium contains goblet ceils. ae a ~ "¢, It has well developed circular smooth muscles. = ‏ا‎ ‎So, ‘d. It has mucoserous glands.in its wall. 20 re . oe ~ 25) Alveolar sacs are characterized by the following: 00

options.A: They are expanded irregular spaces at the distal ends of terminal
options.C: They have smooth muscles in their walls

questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: Alveolar sacs are defined as clusters of alveoli opening into a common expanded space at the terminal ends of the alveolar ducts -- exactly what option A describes -- forming the final, most distal air-containing structures of the respiratory tree before gas exchange occurs across the surrounding alveolar walls. They are lined by simple squamous epithelium (dominated by thin Type I pneumocytes) rather than cuboidal epithelium, essentially lack the smooth muscle found at more proximal levels of the airway tree, and are in fact densely invested with blood capillaries, since this capillary network pressed against the thin squamous lining is precisely what makes gas exchange possible. The histology takeaway is to picture the alveolar sac as the terminal, expanded, capillary-rich air space cluster, distinct from the muscular, cartilage-containing, or goblet-cell-bearing features that instead characterise more proximal conducting airway segments like the bronchiole itself.

distractorNotes.B: Alveolar sacs and alveoli are lined by simple SQUAMOUS epithelium (Type I and Type II pneumocytes), not simple cuboidal epithelium.
distractorNotes.C: Smooth muscle is present at more proximal levels (bronchioles, alveolar ducts, where small muscular sphincters guard the alveolar mouths) but is essentially absent by the level of the alveolar sac itself.
distractorNotes.D: Alveolar sacs are, on the contrary, extremely richly supplied with blood capillaries, since this close capillary-alveolar apposition is the structural basis of gas exchange.

questions.stem: A méntaliy retarded female patient with short stature, primary amenorrhea | and underdeveloped secondary sex organs was asked: to perform karyotyping. Her karyotype would probably be: |
questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: Short stature, primary amenorrhoea, and underdeveloped secondary sexual characteristics are the classic diagnostic triad of Turner syndrome, whose karyotype is 45,X (informally 45,XO) -- a single X chromosome with no second sex chromosome, resulting in ovarian dysgenesis (streak gonads) that prevents normal pubertal development and menstruation. While Turner syndrome's cognitive profile is more accurately described as normal general intelligence with specific non-verbal/spatial learning difficulties rather than global mental retardation, this vignette's overwhelming combination of features (short stature, amenorrhoea, undeveloped secondary sex organs, female sex) still points most specifically and classically to Turner syndrome among the given options.

distractorNotes.A: 47,XXY (Klinefelter's syndrome) describes a genetically male individual (a Y chromosome is present), inconsistent with the female patient described.
distractorNotes.C: The notation '47, XY trisomy 21' describes a genetically male individual with Down syndrome, inconsistent both with the stated female sex and with the specific gonadal/short-stature/amenorrhoea presentation described.
distractorNotes.D: 47,XXX (triple X syndrome) is a possible consideration for a female patient with mild cognitive effects, but it does not classically produce the short stature, primary amenorrhoea, and underdeveloped secondary sex organ triad as specifically as Turner syndrome does.

questions.stem: A patient has an auto immune disease .It may be due to a defect in the lymphocytes produced in the:
variants: [Histo MCQ by Dr.Kandeel [104].pdf p10 #3] A patient has an auto immune disease .it may be due to a defect in the lymphocytes produced in the: :: A) Lymph node B) Spleen C) Palatine tonsil D) Thymus gland
questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: Autoimmune disease can arise from a failure of central immune tolerance, the process by which self-reactive T-lymphocytes are normally eliminated (negative selection) or otherwise inactivated during their maturation within the thymus -- if this thymic selection process is defective, self-reactive T-cells can escape into the peripheral circulation and go on to attack the body's own tissues. This distinguishes the thymus's role as a primary lymphoid organ responsible for T-cell education and self-tolerance from the secondary lymphoid organs (lymph node, spleen, palatine tonsil), where already-mature, already-tolerant lymphocytes go on to encounter antigen and mount immune responses rather than undergoing the initial tolerance-establishing selection process itself.

distractorNotes.A: The lymph node is a secondary lymphoid organ where mature lymphocytes encounter antigen; it is not the site where T-cell self-tolerance is initially established.
distractorNotes.C: The palatine tonsil is a secondary lymphoid organ (part of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue), not the site of T-cell central tolerance selection.

questions.stem: A patient was diagnosed as having chronic myeloid leukemia. His | condition might be due to:

options.B: Deletion of short arm of chromosome 4. 0 |
options.C: Deletion of short arm of chromosome 5

variants: [DPT HISTO MCQ [Cytogenetics] 2023.pdf p3 #8] A patient was diagnosed as having chronic myeloid leukemia. His condition might be due to: :: A) Reciprocal translocation between chromosome 22 and 9 B) Deletion of short arm of chromosome 4 C) Deletion of short arm of chromosome 5 D) Centric fusion of chromosomes 14 and 21

[Histo MCQ by Dr.Kandeel [104].pdf p41 #8] A patient was diagnosed as having chronic myeloid leukemia. His condition might be due to: :: A) Reciprocal translocation between chromosome 22 and B) Deletion of short arm of chromosome C) Deletion of short arm of chromosome D) Centric fusion of chromosomes 14 and 21
questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: Chronic myeloid leukaemia is classically caused by a reciprocal translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22, t(9;22), which creates the abnormally shortened 'Philadelphia chromosome' (the derivative chromosome 22) and fuses the BCR gene on chromosome 22 with the ABL1 gene from chromosome 9, producing a constitutively active BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase that drives uncontrolled myeloid cell proliferation. This specific translocation is one of medicine's most well-established genotype-phenotype correlations, and its discovery was foundational to both cytogenetic diagnosis of leukaemia and the later development of targeted tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy (imatinib). The exam takeaway is to fix 'CML = Philadelphia chromosome = t(9;22)' as an essential, frequently tested cytogenetics-oncology fact.

distractorNotes.B: Deletion of the short arm of chromosome 4 causes Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome, an unrelated congenital disorder, not CML.
distractorNotes.C: Deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5 causes Cri-du-chat syndrome, an unrelated congenital disorder, not CML.
distractorNotes.D: Centric (Robertsonian) fusion of chromosomes 14 and 21 is associated with familial translocation Down syndrome, not CML.

questions.stem: A patient with heart failure, the ejection fraction is:
questions.subject: Physiology

editorialExplanation.explanation: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) is clinically defined by a left ventricular ejection fraction below 40%, reflecting significantly impaired systolic contractile function -- the heart is unable to eject a normal proportion of its end-diastolic volume with each beat. This specific 40% threshold is the standard, most frequently cited cutoff distinguishing reduced-EF heart failure from the normal range (roughly 55-70%) and from heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF, where EF remains normal despite impaired diastolic filling).

distractorNotes.B: 60% falls within the normal ejection fraction range, inconsistent with a diagnosis of reduced-EF heart failure.
distractorNotes.C: 70% is within (or above) the normal ejection fraction range, inconsistent with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.
distractorNotes.D: 80% is a supranormal ejection fraction value, inconsistent with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.

questions.stem: A swab from the buccal mucosa of a newly born infant showed more | than one Barr bodies in the nuclei of nearly all epithelial cells. This condition may be diagnosed as:
variants: [Histo MCQ by Dr.Kandeel [104].pdf p41 #3] A swab from the buccal mucosa of a newly born infant showed more than one Barr bodies in the nuclei of nearly all epithelial cells. This condition may be diagnosed as: :: A) Multiple X syndrome B) Klinefelter syndrome C) Normal female D) Turner syndrome
questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: The number of Barr bodies (inactivated X chromosomes) visible in a cell's nucleus always equals the total number of X chromosomes minus one, since all but one X chromosome is inactivated in every cell. A normal female (46,XX) therefore shows exactly one Barr body, so finding MORE than one Barr body in nearly every epithelial cell indicates the presence of three or more X chromosomes (such as 47,XXX or higher), a pattern grouped under 'multiple X syndrome' (polysomy X). This buccal smear technique is a classic, simple screening method for detecting extra X chromosome material before formal karyotyping confirms the exact constitution.

distractorNotes.B: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) shows only one Barr body, since it has only two X chromosomes, not the multiple Barr bodies described here.
distractorNotes.C: A normal female shows exactly one Barr body, not more than one.
distractorNotes.D: Turner syndrome (45,X) shows NO Barr bodies at all, since there is only a single X chromosome present.

questions.stem: A7 year old child came to the pediatric clinic presenting with a typical picture of acute tonsillitis, choose the true statement related to this case:

options.A: The regional lymph nodes are likely to be inflamed. 8
options.B: Metastatic lymph nodes are likely seen
options.C: Blood film from this patient may present eosinophilia
options.D: Blood film from this patient may present basophilia

questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: Acute tonsillitis classically produces reactive inflammation and enlargement of the regional lymph nodes draining the tonsillar area -- particularly the jugulodigastric (tonsillar) node in the upper deep cervical chain -- a very common and expected clinical finding on examination of a child with this presentation. This reactive lymphadenopathy reflects the immune response mounted by these regional nodes against the infecting organisms, and is a routine part of the clinical picture rather than an unusual or alarming finding in this context. A blood film in this acute bacterial infection would typically be expected to show neutrophilia, the standard response to acute bacterial infection, not eosinophilia or basophilia, and there is no suggestion of malignancy to justify calling any nodal enlargement 'metastatic'.

distractorNotes.B: Describing lymph node enlargement as 'metastatic' implies cancer spread, which is inappropriate and unsupported in a case of simple acute infectious tonsillitis in a child.
distractorNotes.C: Acute bacterial tonsillitis would classically produce neutrophilia on a blood film, not eosinophilia, which is more typical of parasitic infections or allergic conditions.
distractorNotes.D: Acute bacterial tonsillitis would classically produce neutrophilia, not basophilia, on a blood film.

questions.stem: About mediators and vasoactive substances, all of the following are true Except:

options.A: Norepinephrine is a hormone for arteriolar vasoconstriction
options.B: Kinins are hormones for arteriolar vasoconstriction
options.D: Catecholamines and vasopressin are circulating vasoconstrictor substances

questions.subject: Physiology

editorialExplanation.explanation: Kinins, such as bradykinin, are potent VASODILATORS, not vasoconstrictors -- they relax vascular smooth muscle and increase vascular permeability, playing a central role in inflammation and local blood flow regulation, making the claim that they cause arteriolar vasoconstriction the exact opposite of their true physiological action. The other statements are correctly true: norepinephrine, acting through alpha-adrenergic receptors, is a genuine vasoconstrictor; angiotensin II is one of the body's most potent vasoconstrictor hormones; and both catecholamines and vasopressin (ADH, at higher concentrations acting on V1 receptors) function as circulating vasoconstrictor substances. The exam takeaway is to fix kinins firmly in the vasodilator category, alongside substances like histamine and prostaglandins, distinct from the vasoconstrictor group tested in the other options.

distractorNotes.A: Norepinephrine, acting via alpha-1 adrenergic receptors on vascular smooth muscle, is a genuine and potent arteriolar vasoconstrictor.
distractorNotes.C: Angiotensin II is one of the body's most potent circulating vasoconstrictors, a core component of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system's blood pressure regulation.
distractorNotes.D: Both catecholamines (epinephrine/norepinephrine) and vasopressin are genuine circulating vasoconstrictor hormones.

questions.stem: About the cardiac muscle all the following are true except : a, It has low electric resistance of the membrane at the intercalated discs

options.A: It has low electric resistance of the membrane at the intercalated discs
options.C: It obeys the all or none law .
options.D: there is almost a special capillary for each muscle fiber .

questions.subject: Physiology

editorialExplanation.explanation: Cardiac muscle forms a FUNCTIONAL syncytium, not a true (anatomical) syncytium: individual cardiac muscle cells remain structurally distinct, each with its own nucleus and cell membrane, but are electrically coupled via low-resistance gap junctions at the intercalated discs, allowing action potentials to spread rapidly between cells so the tissue behaves AS IF it were a single continuous unit. This is a critical distinction from a true syncytium (a single continuous mass of cytoplasm shared among many nuclei, as seen in skeletal muscle fibres or the placental syncytiotrophoblast), making the claim that cardiac muscle forms a 'true' syncytium the false statement here. The other statements are correct: intercalated discs do have low electrical resistance (via gap junctions), cardiac muscle does obey the all-or-none law (each chamber contracts maximally or not at all, owing to its functional syncytial spread of excitation), and cardiac muscle is exceptionally richly supplied with capillaries, with roughly one capillary per muscle fibre.

distractorNotes.A: True: the intercalated discs' gap junctions provide low electrical resistance, enabling rapid, coordinated spread of excitation between cardiac muscle cells.
distractorNotes.C: True: because excitation spreads through the functional syncytium to the whole chamber, cardiac muscle obeys the all-or-none law at the level of each chamber.
distractorNotes.D: True: cardiac muscle's high, continuous metabolic (oxidative) demand is matched by an unusually dense capillary network, approaching one capillary per muscle fibre.

questions.stem: About the transverse sinus of the serous pericardium mark one correct statement:

options.A: Situated between ascending aorta and SVC
options.B: Present between anterior wall of left atrium and both of ascending aorta and
options.E: The circumflex artery passes to the left through 't

questions.subject: Anatomy

editorialExplanation.explanation: The transverse sinus of the pericardium is the passage lying between the arterial pedicle (ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk) anteriorly and the venous structures (superior vena cava and the roof of the left atrium) posteriorly, formed where the serous pericardium reflects around the great vessels -- 'situated between the ascending aorta and the SVC' is the standard simplified description of this relationship. This space is of major surgical importance because it allows a finger or clamp to be passed behind the great arteries and in front of the great veins, for instance to control blood flow during cardiac surgery. The exam takeaway is to pair the transverse sinus with the arterial-pedicle/venous-structure boundary, distinct from the oblique sinus, which instead sits behind the left atrium bounded by the pulmonary veins.

distractorNotes.C: The transverse sinus is a potential space, not a conduit for a coronary artery; the right coronary artery runs externally in the coronary (atrioventricular) sulcus, unrelated to this sinus.
distractorNotes.D: The coronary sinus lies in the posterior coronary sulcus, related to the region of the oblique sinus, not contained within the transverse sinus.
distractorNotes.E: The circumflex artery runs in the coronary sulcus around the heart's external surface; it does not pass through the pericardial transverse sinus.

questions.stem: According to gene content in chromosomes, autosomes are:

options.D: Control the sex of the individual

variants: [EOY 104 FINALS (answered) (1) (1).pdf p27 #8] According to gene content in chromosomes, autosomes are: :: A) 23 homologous pair of chromosomes B) One pair of chromosomes D) Control the sex of the individual
questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: When chromosomes are classified according to their gene content (what traits their genes actually control), autosomes are defined as the chromosomes that control the body's general somatic (non-sex-determining) characteristics, in contrast to the sex chromosomes, which specifically carry the genes determining an individual's sex and sex-linked traits. This functional classification is distinct from a purely numerical or structural description of chromosomes, matching precisely what this question's specific framing ('according to gene content') is asking for. The exam takeaway is to keep the two classification lenses separate: by NUMBER, humans have 22 autosome pairs plus 1 sex chromosome pair (23 total); by GENE CONTENT/FUNCTION, autosomes control somatic characteristics while sex chromosomes determine sex.

distractorNotes.A: Twenty-three homologous pairs describes the total chromosome complement (including the sex chromosome pair), not autosomes specifically, which number 22 pairs.
distractorNotes.B: Autosomes as a category comprise 22 pairs, not a single pair.
distractorNotes.D: Controlling the sex of the individual is the defining role of the sex chromosomes, not the autosomes.

questions.stem: According to Starling law, the strength of cardiac muscle contraction is directly proportionate to which of the following?

options.D: Degree of stretching of muscle fibres

questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: The Frank-Starling law of the heart states that, within physiological limits, the strength of cardiac muscle contraction is directly related to the initial length of the muscle fibres just before contraction begins -- that is, the degree to which the fibres are stretched by venous filling (preload). Greater diastolic stretch increases the overlap and calcium sensitivity of the actin-myosin contractile apparatus up to an optimal length, producing a more forceful subsequent contraction, which is the physiological basis for the heart automatically matching its output to venous return without needing external neural signals. This length-tension relationship is the single most important, most frequently tested statement of Starling's law in cardiac physiology.

distractorNotes.A: Arterial blood pressure relates to afterload, a separate determinant of cardiac performance from the length-dependent (preload-based) relationship Starling's law describes.
distractorNotes.B: Decreased oxygen supply to the myocardium would impair contractile strength through an entirely different (ischaemic) mechanism, unrelated to fibre stretch.
distractorNotes.C: End-systolic volume is a consequence of the heart's pumping performance, not the variable that Starling's law identifies as directly determining contraction strength.

questions.stem: Achild presented with mental retardation, muscular hypotonia, cardiac abnormalities, small genital organs. You have to think about:
questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: This combination of findings -- mental retardation, muscular hypotonia (a classically prominent early feature), congenital cardiac abnormalities (such as atrioventricular septal defects), and small genital organs -- is a well-recognised presentation of Down syndrome (trisomy 21), one of the most common and most frequently tested multisystem chromosomal disorders. Down syndrome's combination of hypotonia in infancy plus structural heart defects is a particularly classic diagnostic clue pattern taught for early recognition. The exam takeaway is to recognise this specific symptom cluster (hypotonia + cardiac defect + intellectual disability) as pointing to Down syndrome well before dysmorphic facial features are even considered.

distractorNotes.A: Klinefelter's syndrome typically presents at or after puberty with tall stature and small testes, not in infancy with hypotonia and cardiac defects.
distractorNotes.C: Monosomy of chromosome 21 is not a recognised, viable clinical entity presenting this way; it is generally incompatible with survival to term.
distractorNotes.D: Turner syndrome does not typically cause mental retardation (intelligence is usually normal) and presents with short stature and gonadal dysgenesis rather than this cardiac/hypotonia/mental retardation cluster.

editorialExplanation.explanation: All four cardiac valves are closed during the two isovolumetric (isometric) phases of the cardiac cycle -- isovolumetric contraction and isovolumetric relaxation -- since these are precisely the periods where ventricular volume must remain constant, requiring no valve to be open to let blood enter or leave. During isovolumetric relaxation specifically, the semilunar valves have just closed (ending ejection) while the AV valves have not yet opened (since ventricular pressure is still above atrial pressure), leaving all four valves shut as ventricular pressure falls rapidly at constant volume.

distractorNotes.B: During atrial systole, the AV valves are open, allowing the final surge of blood ('atrial kick') into the ventricles -- not all valves are closed.
distractorNotes.C: Protodiastole is the brief transition moment as the semilunar valves are just closing at the end of ejection; the AV valves remain closed too, but this instant is better characterised as the very end of ejection rather than the defining 'all valves closed' isovolumetric phase.

options.E: Esophageal branches

questions.subject: Anatomy

editorialExplanation.explanation: The left subclavian artery is the third branch of the arch of the aorta itself (after the brachiocephalic trunk and the left common carotid artery), not a branch of the descending thoracic aorta, which begins only after the arch ends at the lower border of T4. The descending thoracic aorta's genuine branches include the posterior intercostal arteries (typically the third through eleventh spaces), the subcostal artery, bronchial and oesophageal branches, and small pericardial and mediastinal branches. The takeaway is to keep arch-of-aorta branches (brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid, left subclavian) strictly separate from descending-thoracic-aorta branches (posterior intercostals, subcostal, bronchial, oesophageal).

distractorNotes.A: Posterior intercostal arteries genuinely arise from the descending thoracic aorta, supplying most intercostal spaces below the second.
distractorNotes.B: The subcostal artery, running below the twelfth rib, genuinely arises from the descending thoracic aorta as its most inferior named branch.
distractorNotes.D: Bronchial arteries genuinely arise from the descending thoracic aorta (usually one right, two left) to supply the lung parenchyma via the systemic circulation.
distractorNotes.E: Oesophageal branches genuinely arise directly from the descending thoracic aorta to supply the mid-oesophagus.

questions.stem: All of the followings are causes of pitting edema Except:
questions.subject: Physiology

editorialExplanation.explanation: Longstanding (chronic) lymphatic obstruction produces lymphoedema that becomes characteristically NON-pitting over time, because the chronically stagnant, protein-rich fluid stimulates progressive tissue fibrosis, giving the affected area a firm, non-compressible texture that no longer pits on pressure -- a classic distinguishing clinical feature separating chronic lymphoedema from the pitting oedema of other causes. This contrasts with liver cirrhosis (hypoalbuminaemia and portal hypertension), nutritional (protein-deficiency) oedema, and nephrotic syndrome (severe proteinuria and hypoalbuminaemia), all of which reduce plasma oncotic pressure and produce classic soft, pitting oedema.

distractorNotes.A: Liver cirrhosis causes pitting oedema via hypoalbuminaemia (reduced oncotic pressure) combined with portal hypertension.
distractorNotes.B: Nutritional (protein-deficiency) oedema causes pitting oedema via hypoalbuminaemia and reduced plasma oncotic pressure.
distractorNotes.D: Nephrotic syndrome causes pitting oedema via severe proteinuria leading to hypoalbuminaemia and reduced oncotic pressure.

questions.stem: Amale child at puberty is presented with mental retardation, tall stature, | small testis and widely separated nipples. This condition could be due to: 1

options.C: Loss of Y chromosome during meiosis.
options.D: Non disjunction of the X chromosomes.

questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: This presentation -- mental retardation, tall stature, small testes, and gynecomastia (widely separated nipples reflecting breast tissue development) -- is the classic phenotype of Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY), which most commonly arises from non-disjunction of the X chromosomes during meiosis in either parent, resulting in a gamete carrying an extra X chromosome. This extra X chromosome disrupts normal testicular development and testosterone production, producing the combination of hypogonadism (small testes), eunuchoid tall stature, and gynecomastia classically taught for this condition. The exam takeaway is to associate the Klinefelter phenotype specifically with X chromosome non-disjunction during meiosis, distinguishing this mechanism from autosomal trisomies or losses.

distractorNotes.A: Trisomy of chromosome 21 causes Down syndrome, a different phenotype (present from birth, not one that specifically manifests with these pubertal, hypogonadal features).
distractorNotes.B: Loss of an autosome during mitosis would typically be lethal to the affected cell line or produce a very different, non-viable phenotype, not this specific pubertal presentation.
distractorNotes.C: Loss of the Y chromosome during meiosis would tend toward a Turner-like (45,X) karyotype rather than the extra-X Klinefelter phenotype described.

questions.stem: An effect of myocardial ischemia on the electrical activity of the heart is:

options.B: Inhibition of Na+ - K+ ATPase pump
options.D: Increased the slope of phase 0 of action potential

questions.subject: Physiology

editorialExplanation.explanation: Myocardial ischemia depletes the ATP supply needed to power the energy-dependent Na+-K+ ATPase pump, inhibiting its function and disrupting the normal transmembrane ionic gradients -- intracellular Na+ accumulates while K+ leaks out of the ischemic cells into the extracellular space, altering resting and action potentials in a way that predisposes to arrhythmias. This mechanism directly explains why the extracellular environment around ischemic myocardium actually shows local HYPERkalaemia (not hypokalaemia), and why phase 0 of the action potential becomes DEPRESSED (slower rate of rise), not accelerated, as ATP and normal ionic gradients are compromised.

distractorNotes.A: Myocardial ischemia causes local HYPERkalaemia in the extracellular fluid (from impaired Na+-K+ pump function and K+ leaking out of cells), not hypokalaemia.
distractorNotes.C: Ischemia causes ATP DEPLETION within cardiomyocytes (due to inadequate oxygen supply for aerobic metabolism), not ATP accumulation.
distractorNotes.D: Ischemia typically DECREASES, not increases, the slope of phase 0 depolarization, as the compromised metabolic and ionic environment impairs fast sodium channel function.

questions.stem: Anterior media stinum Space, mark the unacceptable statement:

options.E: Pericardiosternal ligament

questions.subject: Anatomy

editorialExplanation.explanation: The anterior mediastinum's genuine contents are the thymus (or its fatty remnant in adults), the terminal parts of the internal thoracic vessels, sternopericardial ligaments, lymph nodes, loose areolar tissue, and slips of the sternocostalis (transversus thoracis) muscle related to its posterior wall -- the anterior cutaneous branches of the intercostal nerves, by contrast, are chest-wall and skin structures that pierce through near the sternum but are not themselves contents residing within the anterior mediastinal compartment, making this the 'unacceptable' (incorrect) inclusion. The exam takeaway is to distinguish true mediastinal contents (structures that lie within the compartment) from structures that merely pass near or through its boundary on their way to another destination, like the skin.

distractorNotes.A: The thymus gland (or its remnant) is the classic, defining content of the anterior mediastinum.
distractorNotes.B: The terminal portions of the internal thoracic (internal mammary) vessels are genuine anterior mediastinal contents.
distractorNotes.C: Slips of the sternocostalis (transversus thoracis) muscle relate to the posterior aspect of the anterior mediastinum's sternal wall and are genuinely included as content/boundary structures.
distractorNotes.E: The sternopericardial ligaments, anchoring the fibrous pericardium to the posterior surface of the sternum, are a classic named content of the anterior mediastinum.

questions.stem: Arterial blood pressure may be increased by:
questions.subject: Physiology

editorialExplanation.explanation: A decrease in parasympathetic (vagal) tone removes an inhibitory brake on the SA node, allowing heart rate to rise, which increases cardiac output and thereby raises arterial blood pressure. This is the opposite of decreased sympathetic tone (which would reduce vasoconstriction and cardiac stimulation, lowering BP), venodilation (which reduces venous return and preload, lowering cardiac output and BP), and decreased antidiuretic hormone release (which would promote diuresis and reduce blood volume, lowering BP).

distractorNotes.A: Decreased sympathetic tone would reduce vasoconstriction and cardiac stimulation, lowering (not raising) blood pressure.
distractorNotes.B: Venodilation reduces venous return and cardiac preload, tending to lower (not raise) cardiac output and blood pressure.
distractorNotes.D: Decreased antidiuretic hormone release would promote water excretion and reduce blood volume, lowering (not raising) blood pressure.

distractorNotes.A: Decreased sympathetic tone would lower, not raise, blood pressure.
distractorNotes.B: Venodilation reduces venous return and cardiac output, lowering rather than raising blood pressure.
distractorNotes.D: Decreased ADH release would promote diuresis and lower, not raise, blood pressure.

questions.stem: Arterio-venous anastomoses are: a, Direct connection between’ medium sized arteries and veins

options.A: Direct connection between’ medium sized arteries and veins.
options.B: Direct connection between large elastic arteries and large veins.
options.C: Direct connection between arterioles and venules.

questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: Arteriovenous anastomoses are, by histological definition, direct connections specifically between arterioles and venules, allowing blood to bypass the intervening capillary bed entirely -- this small-vessel scale is what allows the shunt to be tightly and rapidly controlled by the dense sympathetic innervation these structures receive, serving functions like thermoregulation in the fingertips, toes, and ear lobes. The other size pairings (medium arteries to veins, or large elastic arteries to large veins) describe a much larger and physiologically distinct scale of vessel than the true AV anastomosis, and AV anastomoses are themselves a bypass mechanism around capillaries, not a type of capillary.

distractorNotes.A: AV anastomoses connect small vessels (arterioles and venules), not medium-sized arteries and veins, which is too large a scale for this rapidly-controlled shunting structure.
distractorNotes.B: Large elastic arteries and large veins are far too large in scale to form the rapidly-regulated, sympathetically-controlled AV anastomosis structure.
distractorNotes.D: AV anastomoses bypass the capillary bed entirely; they are a distinct shunt structure, not a type of blood capillary themselves.

questions.stem: Arterio-venous anastomoses are characterized by:

options.A: Present in tip of fingers and toes

questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: Arteriovenous (AV) anastomoses are specialised vascular shunts that bypass the capillary bed entirely, connecting an arteriole directly to a venule, and they are indeed concentrated in the tips of the fingers and toes (along with the ear lobes and nose), richly innervated by sympathetic vasoconstrictor fibres that open or close them, and involved in regulating blood flow and pressure distribution to these peripheral extremities. Because each of these three statements is independently a genuine, textbook-recognised feature of AV anastomoses -- their characteristic distribution, their dense sympathetic innervation, and their haemodynamic regulatory role -- the correct choice is the combined 'all of the above' option. This structure is central to thermoregulation: opening these shunts diverts blood away from the skin surface to conserve heat, while closing them redirects flow through the capillary bed to promote heat loss.

questions.stem: As regard the standard limb leads of ECG, lead II represents:

options.A: the potential difference between the left arm and the right arm
options.B: the potential difference between the left leg and the left arm
options.C: the potential difference between the left leg and the right arm

questions.subject: Physiology

editorialExplanation.explanation: By Einthoven's triangle convention, standard limb Lead II specifically records the potential difference between the left leg and the right arm, forming one side of the triangle formed by the three limb electrode positions. This is distinct from Lead I (left arm minus right arm) and Lead III (left leg minus left arm), and Lead II's orientation, roughly parallel to the heart's mean electrical axis, is why it typically shows the clearest, most representative P-QRS-T waveform and is the lead most commonly used for basic rhythm monitoring.

distractorNotes.A: The potential difference between the left arm and right arm defines Lead I, not Lead II.
distractorNotes.B: The potential difference between the left leg and left arm defines Lead III, not Lead II.
distractorNotes.D: Since option C correctly describes Lead II, 'none of the above' is incorrect.

questions.stem: As the preload increases, what is the effect on ventricular myocyte?
questions.subject: Physiology

editorialExplanation.explanation: Increased preload stretches the ventricular myocyte's sarcomeres to a greater initial length before contraction begins, which -- via the Frank-Starling length-tension relationship -- improves the overlap and calcium sensitivity of the actin-myosin contractile apparatus and increases the active tension the muscle develops during contraction, up to an optimal length. This is the cellular basis of the whole-heart Frank-Starling mechanism, allowing the heart to automatically match its output to venous return without requiring a change in intrinsic contractility (inotropy), which is instead a separately-regulated property.

distractorNotes.B: Inotropy (intrinsic contractility) is a separate property, primarily regulated by sympathetic tone and calcium handling, not directly changed by preload/stretch itself.
distractorNotes.C: Increased preload INCREASES, not decreases, sarcomere length, since greater ventricular filling stretches the myocardial fibres further.
distractorNotes.D: Increased preload does not directly decrease the velocity of shortening at a given afterload; that relationship (decreased shortening velocity) is instead classically associated with increased AFTERLOAD, not preload.

At any time, the greatest fraction of blood volume is present in the:
questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: Veins and venules together hold the largest share of total circulating blood volume at any given moment, roughly 60-70%, functioning as a low-pressure capacitance reservoir that can expand or contract to buffer changes in blood volume and adjust venous return to the heart. This is in contrast to arteries (roughly 10-15% of blood volume, built for rapid, low-volume distribution under high pressure) and capillaries (only about 5%, since they exist for exchange rather than storage). The exam takeaway is to remember veins as the blood volume 'reservoir' of the circulatory system, holding the majority share at rest.

distractorNotes.A: The heart holds only a modest fraction of total blood volume at any instant, far less than the venous system.
distractorNotes.B: Arteries hold a moderate share (roughly 10-15%) of total blood volume, considerably less than the venous system's majority share.
distractorNotes.D: Capillaries hold only about 5% of total blood volume, the smallest major compartment, since they function for exchange rather than storage.

editorialExplanation.explanation: The superior vena cava is formed by the union of the two brachiocephalic veins behind the lower border of the FIRST right costal cartilage, a distinctly higher level than the sternal angle (which corresponds to the second costal cartilage), making 'the SVC begins' at the sternal angle the false statement among these otherwise-correct landmarks. The sternal angle (of Louis) is instead the anterior surface marker for a cluster of other genuinely coincident events: the second costal cartilage articulating with the sternum, the tracheal bifurcation, the beginning of the descending aorta (arch ending), and the end of the superior mediastinum, all occurring near the T4/T5 vertebral level posteriorly. The exam takeaway is to keep the SVC's formation level (1st right costal cartilage, higher) distinct from the cluster of sternal-angle-level events (2nd costal cartilage and below).

distractorNotes.A: True: the second costal cartilage articulates with the sternum precisely at the sternal angle, the manubriosternal joint.
distractorNotes.B: True: the trachea bifurcates into the two main bronchi at the level of the sternal angle (T4/T5 disc posteriorly).
distractorNotes.C: True: the arch of the aorta transitions into the descending aorta (i.e. the arch 'ends'/'begins' its posterior continuation) at this same T4 level.
distractorNotes.E: True: the sternal angle plane marks the inferior boundary of the superior mediastinum by definition.

editorialExplanation.explanation: It is the SECOND rib (via its costal cartilage) that articulates with the sternum at the sternal angle -- the manubriosternal joint is, by definition, the articulation point for the second costal cartilage, which is precisely why the sternal angle is used clinically to count ribs starting from the second. The first rib, by contrast, articulates directly with the manubrium itself, above (not at) the sternal angle, making the claim that 'the first rib articulates with sternum' at this level a clear, confidently identifiable swap error. The other statements are correct: the arch of the aorta transitions to the descending aorta at this level, the trachea bifurcates here, and the azygos vein arches into the superior vena cava at approximately this level too.

distractorNotes.C: True: the trachea bifurcates into the two main bronchi at the sternal angle level.
distractorNotes.D: True: the azygos vein arches forward over the root of the right lung to enter the superior vena cava at approximately this level.

questions.stem: AV valves are open during which of the following phases of cardiac cycle?
questions.subject: Physiology

editorialExplanation.explanation: The atrioventricular valves are open during atrial systole, allowing the final, active surge of blood ('atrial kick') to be pushed from the contracting atria into the already largely-filled ventricles just before ventricular systole begins. This is distinct from isometric (isovolumetric) contraction, protodiastole, and maximum ejection, all of which occur during ventricular systole, when the AV valves are firmly closed to prevent backflow of blood into the atria as ventricular pressure rises and ejects blood into the great arteries.

distractorNotes.A: During isometric (isovolumetric) contraction, all four valves, including the AV valves, are closed.
distractorNotes.C: During protodiastole, the AV valves remain closed, just as the semilunar valves are closing at the end of ejection.
distractorNotes.D: During maximum ejection, the AV valves remain closed throughout ventricular systole to prevent backflow into the atria.

questions.stem: Based on the following values, the flow of fluid out of the capillarics will be zero if the average interstitial hydrostatic pressure is : 1 Average capillary hydrostatic pressure = 18 mmHg Average capillary oncolic pressure = 27 mmHg Average interstitial oncotic pressure = 7 mmbg
questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: Net filtration is zero when the outward Starling forces exactly balance the inward ones: (capillary hydrostatic pressure + interstitial oncotic pressure) must equal (interstitial hydrostatic pressure + capillary oncotic pressure). Plugging in the given values: 18 + 7 = Pi + 27, which solves to Pi = -2 mmHg -- a negative interstitial hydrostatic pressure, consistent with the normal physiological finding that interstitial fluid pressure in most tissues is slightly sub-atmospheric (negative). The magnitude of this answer, 2 mmHg, matches option C once the negative sign (very commonly lost in OCR extraction of minus signs) is accounted for, while option D's explicit '+2 mmHg' represents the wrong sign for the calculated balance point.

distractorNotes.A: 4 mmHg does not satisfy the balance equation 18 + 7 = Pi + 27 for any sign convention.
distractorNotes.B: 0 mmHg does not balance the equation either: with Pi = 0, the net filtration pressure would be 18 + 7 - 0 - 27 = -2 mmHg (net absorption, not zero flow).
distractorNotes.D: The magnitude matches the calculated answer, but the required interstitial hydrostatic pressure for zero net flow is negative (-2 mmHg), not positive, since 18 + 7 = -2 + 27 balances correctly while 18 + 7 = +2 + 27 does not.

questions.stem: Blood flows into the coronary arteries arises from the:
questions.subject: Anatomy

editorialExplanation.explanation: The coronary arteries arise from the aortic sinuses (of Valsalva), small dilations located just above the aortic valve at the root of the ascending aorta -- specifically the right and left coronary arteries arise from the right and left posterior aortic sinuses respectively. Coronary filling therefore depends on the ascending aorta's pressure and occurs predominantly during diastole, when the aortic valve cusps are closed and blood in the sinuses is not being swept past the coronary ostia into the ventricle. The exam takeaway is to anchor coronary artery origin specifically to the ascending aorta's root/sinuses, not the arch, descending aorta, or any other great vessel.

distractorNotes.A: The descending aorta lies well beyond the aortic sinuses and gives rise to intercostal, subcostal, bronchial, and oesophageal branches, not the coronary arteries.
distractorNotes.C: The pulmonary trunk carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs and plays no role in coronary artery origin (the rare congenital exception, ALCAPA, is a pathology, not normal anatomy).
distractorNotes.D: The superior vena cava is a systemic vein returning blood to the right atrium; it has no arterial branches and cannot be the source of the coronary arteries.

questions.stem: Blood sinusoids are characterized by the following:

options.A: Have no pores in their wall
options.B: Endcthelial cells are separated by minimal intercellular spaces
options.D: Macrophages are found among or outside their wall

variants: [Histo MCQ by Dr.Kandeel [104].pdf p19 #24] Blood sinusoids are characterized by the following: :: A) Have no pores in their wall B) Endothelial cells are separated by minimal intercellular spaces C) Have continuous basement membrane D) Macrophages are found among or outside their wall
[DPT HISTO MCQ [Cardiovascular].pdf p3 #24] Blood sinusoids are characterized by the following: :: A) Have no pores in their wall D) Macrophages are found among or outside their wail
questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: A defining histological feature of blood sinusoids is the presence of macrophages sitting either within the sinusoidal wall itself or immediately outside it -- the classic example being Kupffer cells lodged within the lining of liver sinusoids, and macrophages of the splenic cords positioned just outside the wall of splenic sinusoids. This intimate macrophage association reflects the sinusoid's role in organs (liver, spleen, bone marrow, some endocrine glands) where blood needs close surveillance and filtering, which the sinusoid's unusually open, slow-flow architecture is built to support. The exam takeaway is to treat 'macrophages in/around the wall' as sinusoids' signature identifying feature, distinct from the wide intercellular gaps, discontinuous basement membrane, and large irregular lumen that describe their structure but are shared in degree with fenestrated capillaries.

distractorNotes.A: Sinusoids characteristically DO have large pores/gaps in their wall -- often without even a covering diaphragm -- the opposite of having no pores.
distractorNotes.B: Sinusoidal endothelial cells are separated by wide, not minimal, intercellular spaces, which is precisely what allows even large molecules and cells to pass through the wall.
distractorNotes.C: Sinusoids characteristically have a discontinuous or even absent basement membrane, not a continuous one -- this is one of the key features distinguishing them from fenestrated capillaries.

editorialExplanation.explanation: Billroth cords (splenic cords) are the cellular cords of the spleen's red pulp, richly infiltrated with blood cells -- red blood cells, macrophages, lymphocytes, and plasma cells -- reflecting their function as the site where the spleen filters and screens circulating blood, removing aged or damaged erythrocytes. This is an exclusively splenic structure, not found in lymph nodes at all, and is unrelated to the central arteriole (a white pulp landmark) or to the spaces between lymphoid follicles (an unrelated description).

distractorNotes.A: Billroth cords are found in the red pulp of the SPLEEN, not in the stroma of lymph nodes.
distractorNotes.C: This does not describe Billroth cords; it is an unrelated, imprecise description not matching the standard definition of splenic cords.

editorialExplanation.explanation: The paracortex is the deep (inner) part of the lymph node's cortex, situated between the outer cortex (containing B-lymphocyte follicles) and the medulla, and it is specifically rich in T-lymphocytes, earning it the alternative name 'thymus-dependent zone'. This T-cell-rich paracortex is also where specialised high endothelial post-capillary venules are located, allowing circulating lymphocytes to enter the lymph node directly from the bloodstream. The exam takeaway is to fix the paracortex specifically as the T-cell zone, distinct from the outer cortex's B-cell follicles and the medulla's plasma-cell-rich cords.

distractorNotes.B: Littoral cells are a spleen-specific term for the macrophage-like cells lining splenic sinusoids; lymph node sinuses are lined by a different type of sinus-lining reticuloendothelial cell.
distractorNotes.C: Efferent lymphatic vessels drain a lymph node through its CONCAVE surface (the hilum), not the convex surface -- afferent vessels instead pierce the capsule at multiple points on the convex surface.

editorialExplanation.explanation: Chronotropism (from the Greek 'chronos', time) refers specifically to a change in heart rate/rhythm, matching the property of rhythmicity -- the SA node's ability to spontaneously generate the heartbeat's timing. This is one of four classic cardiac physiological properties tested together as a set: chronotropic effects change rate/rhythmicity, dromotropic effects change conduction velocity, bathmotropic effects change excitability/threshold, and inotropic effects change contractile force -- a frequently tested vocabulary distinction.

distractorNotes.B: Conductivity (conduction velocity through the heart) is described by the term dromotropism, not chronotropism.
distractorNotes.C: Excitability (threshold for triggering an action potential) is described by the term bathmotropism, not chronotropism.
distractorNotes.D: Contractility (force of contraction) is described by the term inotropism, not chronotropism.

questions.stem: Compared with the apex of the lung, the base of the lung has 3
questions.subject: Anatomy

editorialExplanation.explanation: In an upright lung, blood flow (perfusion) increases much more steeply from apex to base than ventilation does, so the base ends up with a lower ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) ratio than the apex, meaning base capillary blood spends relatively more of its exchange 'diluted' toward mixed venous gas composition. This lower V/Q at the base translates into a relatively higher capillary PCO2 (and lower PO2) compared with the apex, where the high V/Q ratio pulls alveolar and capillary gas composition closer to that of inspired air (higher PO2, lower PCO2). The exam takeaway is the classic West zone gradient: apex has high V/Q (like dead space, high PO2/low PCO2), base has low V/Q (like a shunt, lower PO2/higher PCO2), even though absolute ventilation and perfusion are both greater at the base.

distractorNotes.C: The base has a LOWER, not higher, V/Q ratio than the apex, since perfusion rises faster than ventilation going down the lung.
distractorNotes.D: The V/Q ratio changes substantially from apex to base in the upright lung; it is not the same at both locations.

questions.stem: Concerning breathing all true except:

options.A: Breathing is controlled by the autonomic nervous system
options.B: The phrenic nerve is a Cranial nerve
options.C: The diaphragm is active during quiet inspiration
options.D: The intercostal muscles are innervated by thoracic spinal nerves

questions.subject: Anatomy

editorialExplanation.explanation: The phrenic nerve is unambiguously a spinal nerve, formed mainly from the fourth cervical spinal nerve root with contributions from the third and fifth (C3, C4, C5) -- it is not one of the twelve cranial nerves, making this a clear and confident factual error. The other statements are true: the respiratory muscles (diaphragm, intercostals) are skeletal muscles controlled by somatic motor neurons whose activity is paced by the brainstem's automatic rhythm-generating centres; the diaphragm is indeed the principal active muscle of quiet inspiration; and the intercostal muscles are innervated by the intercostal nerves, which are themselves the anterior rami of the thoracic spinal nerves. The exam takeaway is to never confuse the phrenic nerve's cervical spinal origin with a cranial nerve, a mistake this option makes outright.

distractorNotes.A: Respiratory rhythm is generated and modulated by brainstem centres acting through somatic motor pathways to skeletal respiratory muscles; while debatable in exact phrasing, it is a far less clear-cut error than mislabelling the phrenic nerve as cranial.
distractorNotes.C: True: the diaphragm is the principal, most active muscle of quiet (resting) inspiration.
distractorNotes.D: True: the intercostal muscles are innervated by the intercostal nerves, which are the anterior (ventral) rami of the thoracic spinal nerves T1-T11.

questions.stem: Concerning laminar blood flow, one is incorrect:
Concerning large veins, which one of the following statements is not true?

options.A: Its adventitia may contain smooth muscles. B- They have well defined internal elastic lamina

questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: Valves are a characteristic feature of medium-sized veins, particularly in the limbs (especially the lower limb), where they prevent the backflow of blood against gravity -- but large veins such as the inferior and superior venae cavae, the portal vein, and other great veins characteristically LACK valves, making this the false statement specifically for large veins as the stem asks. The other statements are correct for large veins: their adventitia may indeed contain longitudinal smooth muscle bundles (a recognised feature, e.g. of the inferior vena cava), and their thin media does contain some elastic fibres alongside smooth muscle, even though large veins generally lack a well-defined internal elastic lamina like arteries do.

distractorNotes.A: True: the tunica adventitia of large veins, such as the inferior vena cava, may contain bundles of longitudinal smooth muscle, an unusual feature not typically seen in the adventitia of comparably-sized arteries.
distractorNotes.D: True: the thin tunica media of large veins does contain some elastic fibres interspersed among the smooth muscle, even without forming a distinct, well-defined elastic lamina.
