questions.stem: Concerning respiration: : a, expiratory muscles act during normal expiration

options.A: expiratory muscles act during normal expiration.
options.B: diaphragm is the only respiratory muscle.
options.C: contraction of external intercostals muscle increase antero-post diameter.

questions.subject: Anatomy

editorialExplanation.explanation: Contraction of the external intercostal muscles elevates the ribs (the 'pump-handle' and 'bucket-handle' movements), which genuinely increases both the anteroposterior and transverse diameters of the thoracic cage during inspiration -- making this the one clearly correct statement among the options. Normal (quiet) expiration is passive, driven by elastic recoil, so expiratory muscles are not active during it, which is why the first statement is false; likewise the diaphragm is the principal but not the sole respiratory muscle (external intercostals contribute even at rest), making the second statement false too. The exam takeaway is to keep 'muscles active in quiet breathing' (diaphragm, external intercostals) separate from 'muscles active only in forced breathing' (internal intercostals, abdominals, scalenes, sternocleidomastoid).

distractorNotes.A: False: expiratory muscles (internal intercostals, abdominal wall muscles) are recruited only for forced/active expiration, not normal quiet expiration, which is passive.
distractorNotes.B: False: the diaphragm is the principal inspiratory muscle but not the only one -- the external intercostals also contribute during quiet breathing.
distractorNotes.D: As extracted this statement is incomplete (it does not say under what conditions the scalenes contract), but the scalene muscles are classically accessory inspiratory muscles recruited in forced, not quiet, breathing.

questions.stem: Concerning the atrial pressure curve a, c-wave occurs during atrial systole

options.B: v-wave occurs during isovolumetric contraction phase
options.C: a-wave precedes the first heart sound
options.D: yv-wave occurs during the ventricular filling phases 00 cont: q

questions.subject: Physiology

editorialExplanation.explanation: The a-wave of the atrial pressure curve is generated by atrial contraction (atrial systole) itself, which occurs just before ventricular systole begins -- and since the first heart sound (S1) marks the closure of the AV valves at the very start of ventricular systole, the a-wave necessarily precedes S1 in the correct chronological sequence of the cardiac cycle. The c-wave, by contrast, is caused by the AV valves bulging back into the atria at the very onset of ventricular systole (isovolumetric contraction), occurring AFTER atrial systole has ended, not during it; and the v-wave builds up from continued venous filling of the atria while the AV valves remain closed during ventricular systole, peaking near the end of systole (not during isovolumetric contraction, and not during the ventricular filling phase, when atrial pressure is instead falling as the atria empty into the ventricles).

distractorNotes.A: The c-wave occurs just after atrial systole has ended, at the onset of ventricular systole (isovolumetric contraction), not during atrial systole itself.
distractorNotes.B: The v-wave builds up during ventricular systole (while the AV valves are closed) and peaks near its end, not during the isovolumetric contraction phase specifically.
distractorNotes.D: The v-wave peaks near the end of ventricular systole and then falls (the y descent) as the AV valves open and rapid ventricular filling begins -- atrial pressure is decreasing, not rising, during the actual filling phase.

questions.stem: Concerning the diaphragm all true EXCEPT:

options.A: Develops from the septum transversum and cervical myotomes
options.B: Receives a nerve supply from both the phrenic and intercostal nerves
options.C: An opening in the central tendon transmits the inferior vena cava
options.D: The inferior vena cava passes through the diaphragm at the level of the T12
options.E: The aorta passes through the diaphragm behind the median arcuate

questions.subject: Anatomy

editorialExplanation.explanation: The inferior vena cava passes through the diaphragm at the level of the eighth thoracic vertebra (T8), through the caval opening in the central tendon -- not at T12, which is instead the level of the aortic hiatus, transmitting the aorta and thoracic duct. Swapping these two diaphragmatic-opening levels is a classic, confidently identifiable error, making this the false statement. The other statements are standard, correct diaphragm facts: it develops embryologically from the septum transversum plus contributions including the cervical myotomes (explaining the phrenic nerve's cervical origin), it receives motor supply from the phrenic nerves and a sensory contribution from the lower intercostal nerves at its periphery, the caval opening in the central tendon does transmit the inferior vena cava, and the aortic hiatus does lie behind the median arcuate ligament (formed by the crura).

distractorNotes.A: True: the diaphragm's composite embryological origin (septum transversum, pleuroperitoneal membranes, dorsal oesophageal mesentery, and body wall/cervical myotomes) is why its motor nerve, the phrenic, originates from cervical spinal segments despite the diaphragm's thoracoabdominal position.
distractorNotes.B: True: the diaphragm's central part is supplied motorically by the phrenic nerves, while its peripheral costal part also receives sensory contributions from the lower intercostal nerves.
distractorNotes.C: True: the caval opening, located in the diaphragm's central tendon at the T8 level, transmits the inferior vena cava.
distractorNotes.E: True: the aortic hiatus lies behind (deep to) the median arcuate ligament, formed by the fibrous arch connecting the diaphragm's two crura, at the T12 level.

questions.stem: Concerning the ECG of an aciult human, all are true EXCEPT:

options.A: The P-wave coincides with depolarization of the atria
options.B: P-R interval of 0.3 seconds indicates impaired conduction
options.C: The R-wave coincides with depolarization of the apex of the heart
options.D: The Q-wave coincides with cleoolarization of the atria

questions.subject: Physiology

editorialExplanation.explanation: The Q wave is part of the QRS complex and reflects early ventricular (specifically septal) depolarization, not atrial depolarization -- atrial depolarization is represented exclusively by the P wave, which precedes the QRS complex entirely. This makes the claim that the Q wave coincides with atrial depolarization a clear, confidently identifiable error. The other statements are correctly true: the P wave does represent atrial depolarization, a PR interval of 0.3 seconds is indeed prolonged beyond the normal 0.12-0.20 second range and indicates impaired (delayed) AV conduction, and the R wave is commonly associated with the depolarization wavefront reaching the ventricular apex region early in the QRS sequence via the rapidly-conducting Purkinje fibres there.

distractorNotes.A: True: the P wave represents atrial depolarization.
distractorNotes.B: True: a PR interval of 0.3 seconds exceeds the normal range (0.12-0.20 seconds) and indicates delayed (impaired) AV nodal conduction, as in first-degree heart block.
distractorNotes.C: True: the ventricular apex is among the first regions to depolarize (via the rapidly-conducting Purkinje network reaching it early), contributing significantly to the R wave.

options.A: It is a muscle of inspiration
options.B: Its fibers are directed downward and forward
options.D: It extends from the rib tubercle to the costochondral junction
options.C: The typical thoracic vertebra articulates with the numerically corresponding

questions.subject: Anatomy

editorialExplanation.explanation: This option describes a fact about typical thoracic vertebra-to-rib articulation (and even then, oversimplifies it: a typical thoracic vertebra actually articulates with two ribs via superior and inferior costal demifacets on its body, not simply 'the numerically corresponding' rib alone) -- it is an unrelated vertebral-column fact that does not belong among statements about the external intercostal muscle's own action, fibre direction, and attachments, making it the clear outlier and the intended incorrect answer. The other three statements are standard, correct facts about the external intercostal muscle: it is a muscle of inspiration, its fibres run obliquely downward and forward, and it extends from the tubercle of the rib above posteriorly to the costochondral junction anteriorly (continuing anteriorly as the anterior intercostal membrane).

distractorNotes.A: True: the external intercostal muscle elevates the ribs, making it an inspiratory muscle.
distractorNotes.B: True: the external intercostal muscle's fibres run obliquely downward and forward, in the 'hands in front pockets' direction.
distractorNotes.D: True: the external intercostal muscle spans from the rib tubercle posteriorly to the costochondral junction anteriorly, where the anterior intercostal membrane continues its fibre direction to the sternum.

questions.stem: Concerning the intercostal and subcostal arteries, which of the following is true?

options.A: They lie highest in the costal groove
options.B: First two posterior intercostal arteries are indirect branches of costocervical
options.C: Posterior intercostal arteries are indirect branches of thyrocervical trunk
options.D: All anterior intercostal arteries are direct branches from internal thoracic and
options.E: Subcostal artery is a direct branch from abdominal aorta

questions.subject: Anatomy

editorialExplanation.explanation: The posterior intercostal arteries supplying the first two intercostal spaces do not arise directly from the descending thoracic aorta; instead they come from the superior (supreme) intercostal artery, which is itself a branch of the costocervical trunk off the subclavian artery -- making them indirect branches of the costocervical trunk, exactly as this option states. This is a well-known exception to the general rule that posterior intercostal arteries (spaces 3-11) arise directly from the descending thoracic aorta, and it exists because the aorta has not yet reached the level of the upper two intercostal spaces at the point it enters the thorax. The exam takeaway is to remember this specific exception (spaces 1-2 via costocervical trunk/superior intercostal artery) as distinct from the general rule (spaces 3-11 direct from the descending thoracic aorta).

distractorNotes.A: The standard costal-groove order from superior to inferior is vein, artery, then nerve (VAN) -- so the vein, not the artery, lies highest in the groove.
distractorNotes.C: The relevant subclavian branch for the first two posterior intercostal arteries is the costocervical trunk, not the thyrocervical trunk -- a classic distractor swap between these two similarly-named subclavian branches.
distractorNotes.D: Only the anterior intercostal arteries of the upper six spaces are direct branches of the internal thoracic artery; those of the lower spaces (roughly 7-9) instead arise indirectly via the musculophrenic artery, a terminal branch of the internal thoracic artery, so 'all' overstates this.
distractorNotes.E: The subcostal artery is the last, most inferior branch of the DESCENDING THORACIC aorta, given off just above the diaphragm, not a branch of the abdominal aorta, which begins only after the aorta has passed through the diaphragm.

questions.stem: Concerning the left ventricle, select the incorrect statement:

options.A: Itis three times thicker than the right ventricle
options.B: The trabeculae carnae are more than those of the ‘so ventricle
options.D: The left coronary artery supplies the major part of the interventricular septum

questions.subject: Anatomy

editorialExplanation.explanation: The trabeculae carneae (muscular ridges lining the ventricular cavity) are coarser and more prominent in the right ventricle than in the left, not the other way round, so the statement that the left ventricle's are 'more than' the right ventricle's is false. Mechanistically, the right ventricle is a low-pressure volume pump whose wall relies more on trabecular architecture for contraction, while the thicker, high-pressure left ventricle has comparatively smoother inner walls apart from its papillary muscles. The takeaway is that thickness and trabeculation do not track together across the two ventricles: the left ventricle is the thicker chamber (about three times the right) but the right ventricle is the more heavily trabeculated one.

distractorNotes.A: Correctly true: the left ventricle wall is roughly three times thicker than the right, since it must generate systemic (not pulmonary) pressures.
distractorNotes.D: Correctly true: the left coronary artery's anterior interventricular (LAD) branch supplies the anterior two-thirds of the interventricular septum in most hearts.

questions.stem: Concerning the oblique sinus of the serous pericardium, indicate the accepted statement:

options.A: Situated in front of left atrium
options.B: Behind left atrium and is bounded by the 4 pulmonary veins
options.C: Behind left atrium and bounded by the pulmonary veins and both of superior
options.D: It lodges the great cardiac vein
options.E: It transmits the posterior interventricular artery

questions.subject: Anatomy

editorialExplanation.explanation: The oblique sinus of the pericardium is a cul-de-sac lying behind the left atrium, formed by the reflection of the serous pericardium around the pulmonary veins, and is classically described as bounded by the four pulmonary veins (two right, two left) entering the back of the left atrium. This recess is closed on all sides except for a narrow inferior opening, and its posterior relations (oesophagus and descending aorta) are exactly what the pericardium's oblique sinus separates from the heart's posterior surface. The exam takeaway is to keep the oblique sinus's landmark (behind the left atrium, bounded by the pulmonary veins) distinct from the transverse sinus's landmark (between the great arteries and great veins anteriorly/posteriorly).

distractorNotes.A: The oblique sinus lies behind, not in front of, the left atrium.
distractorNotes.C: While some descriptions extend the oblique sinus's boundary to include a nearby great vein (the inferior vena cava) alongside the pulmonary veins, this option's truncated wording risks overstating that boundary (e.g. by including the superior vena cava, which is not part of it), making the simpler, unambiguously correct pulmonary-veins description the safer choice.
distractorNotes.D: The great cardiac vein runs in the anterior interventricular groove and then the coronary sulcus toward the coronary sinus, unrelated to the oblique sinus.
distractorNotes.E: The posterior interventricular artery runs externally in the posterior interventricular groove on the diaphragmatic surface of the heart, not through the pericardial oblique sinus.

questions.stem: Concerning the oesophagus all true EXCEPT:

options.B: In the thorax passes behind the left main bronchus
options.C: It passes through the oesophageal opening of the diaphragm at the level of
options.D: Is lined by transitional epithelium in the lower one-third
options.E: Drains all of its blood into the azygos and hemiazygos veins

questions.subject: Anatomy

editorialExplanation.explanation: The oesophagus is lined throughout its length by non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium, changing abruptly to simple columnar (gastric-type) epithelium only exactly at the oesophagogastric junction -- 'transitional epithelium' is an entirely different, unrelated tissue type (urothelium) found lining the urinary tract (renal pelvis, ureters, bladder, part of the urethra), never the oesophagus at any level. This makes the statement definitively false regardless of which third of the oesophagus is being described. The exam takeaway is to keep the two commonly confused epithelium types straight: stratified squamous protects the oesophagus (and skin, oral cavity, anal canal) from mechanical abrasion, while transitional epithelium is a distensibility-adapted lining unique to the urinary tract.

distractorNotes.A: The oesophagus's length is commonly cited as approximately 25 cm anatomically, though endoscopic/incisor-based measurements (used clinically) can approach 40 cm depending on the reference point -- this option's truth depends on which convention the source uses and is less definitively false than the epithelium claim.
distractorNotes.B: True: in the thorax, the oesophagus passes posterior to the left main bronchus after crossing behind the tracheal bifurcation.

editorialExplanation.explanation: The end-systolic pressure-volume relationship (ESPVR) specifically represents the maximal ACTIVE tension-generating capacity of the ventricle (a measure of its contractile state/contractility) at end-systole, not the 'total' tension, which would misleadingly suggest a combination of both active and passive components together. This distinction matters because ESPVR's slope is used clinically and experimentally as a load-independent index of contractility, a concept that depends specifically on isolating the active contractile component, not a generic 'total' tension figure. The other statements are correct: the EDPVR does represent the ventricle's passive elastic tension as it fills (analogous to the passive length-tension curve of isolated resting muscle), the end-diastolic volume is the standard practical measure of preload, and the end-systolic pressure is the standard practical measure of afterload.

distractorNotes.A: True: the EDPVR reflects the passive tension developed by the resting, non-contracting ventricular wall as it is stretched by filling, analogous to a passive length-tension curve.
distractorNotes.C: True: end-diastolic volume is the standard clinical and experimental proxy for preload.
distractorNotes.D: True: end-systolic pressure is the standard clinical and experimental proxy for afterload.

questions.stem: Concerning the thymus, which of the following is correct? 1

options.A: Its reticular epithelial cells are mesodermal and produce reticular fibres. |
options.B: The blood thymic barrier is found in the medulla
options.C: Ithas plasma cells and afferent lymphatic vessels. |
options.D: Cortex of each thymic lobule appears darker in staining than medulla

questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: The thymic cortex appears distinctly darker (more densely basophilic) on histological staining than the medulla, because the cortex is densely packed with numerous small, actively dividing and maturing lymphocytes (thymocytes), while the medulla contains fewer, more mature lymphocytes along with more epithelial reticular cells and the characteristic eosinophilic Hassall's corpuscles, giving it a comparatively paler appearance. This staining contrast is one of the most basic and reliable ways to orient a thymus histology slide at low power. The other statements are false: the thymus's epithelial reticular cells are endodermal (not mesodermal) in origin, the blood-thymic barrier is a cortical (not medullary) feature protecting developing thymocytes there, and the thymus characteristically lacks both plasma cells and afferent lymphatic vessels altogether.

distractorNotes.A: Thymic epithelial reticular cells derive embryologically from the endoderm of the third pharyngeal pouch, not from mesoderm.
distractorNotes.B: The blood-thymic barrier is a feature of the thymic CORTEX, protecting developing thymocytes there from blood-borne antigens; the medulla lacks this same strict barrier.
distractorNotes.C: The thymus characteristically lacks both plasma cells and afferent lymphatic vessels, since it is a primary lymphoid organ where lymphocytes mature rather than one where immune responses or antigen filtering occur.

questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: The upper pair of folds in the larynx are the vestibular (false vocal) folds, whose primary role is protective -- helping to close off the airway and prevent foreign material, food, or liquid from entering the larynx and trachea below, distinct from the lower pair (the true vocal cords), whose specialised role is phonation (sound production). The true vocal cords, not the vestibular folds, are the ones containing the well-developed elastic vocal ligament and being covered by the mechanically durable non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium needed to withstand the friction of vibration during speech; the vestibular folds instead are typically covered by respiratory-type epithelium and lack this same prominent elastic ligament.

distractorNotes.A: The true vocal cords are the LOWER pair of folds, specialised for phonation; the upper pair are the false (vestibular) folds.
distractorNotes.B: The well-developed elastic vocal ligament is a feature of the lower, true vocal cords, not the upper, false vocal folds.
distractorNotes.C: The mechanically durable non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium covering is a feature of the true vocal cords (built to withstand vibrational friction), not the vestibular folds, which are typically covered by respiratory-type epithelium.

questions.stem: Conduction speed is highest in the:
questions.subject: Anatomy

editorialExplanation.explanation: Conduction velocity through the cardiac conduction system is fastest in the Purkinje fibres, reaching roughly 2-4 m/s, because their large diameter and abundant gap junctions let the depolarising wavefront spread almost instantly to the ventricular myocardium. This speed is functionally essential: it lets the Purkinje network deliver a near-simultaneous stimulus to both ventricles so they contract together rather than as a slow, disorganised wave. The takeaway ranking, from fastest to slowest, is Purkinje > atrial/internodal pathways > SA node > AV node, with the AV node deliberately the slowest link to allow ventricular filling before systole.

distractorNotes.A: The SA node conducts slowly relative to Purkinje tissue; its role is pacemaking, not rapid conduction.
distractorNotes.B: Internodal atrial bundles conduct faster than nodal tissue but far slower than Purkinje fibres.
distractorNotes.C: The AV node is the slowest-conducting tissue in the heart, the opposite of this question's answer.

questions.stem: Conduction speed is slowest in the:
questions.subject: Anatomy

editorialExplanation.explanation: The AV node has the slowest conduction velocity in the heart, on the order of 0.05 m/s, because its small-diameter fibres and sparse gap junctions produce a deliberate conduction delay. This delay is physiologically purposeful: it gives the atria time to finish contracting and empty into the ventricles (the 'atrial kick') before the ventricles are electrically activated, optimising ventricular filling and stroke volume. The broader takeaway is that the conduction system trades speed for timing control at the AV node, in contrast to the Purkinje fibres, which are optimised purely for speed.

distractorNotes.A: The SA node conducts faster than the AV node; it is the pacemaker, not the delay point.
distractorNotes.B: Atrial pathways conduct impulses relatively quickly across the atria compared with the AV node.
distractorNotes.D: The Purkinje system is the fastest-conducting tissue in the heart, the opposite extreme from this question's answer.

editorialExplanation.explanation: Down syndrome is defined as trisomy 21, the presence of three copies (rather than the normal two) of chromosome 21, resulting in 47 total chromosomes rather than the normal 46. This is a numerical chromosomal aberration affecting a single specific autosome, entirely distinct from triploidy (which involves an extra COMPLETE set of all chromosomes, 69 total) and from any aberration of the sex chromosomes, since chromosome 21 is an autosome. The exam takeaway is to fix 'Down syndrome = trisomy 21 = 47 chromosomes, one autosome triplicated' as the precise definitional fact, distinguishing it from other numerical aberration types.

distractorNotes.A: Triploidy refers to an extra complete haploid set of all chromosomes (69 total), a distinct and generally non-viable condition, not what causes Down syndrome.
distractorNotes.B: Down syndrome cells contain 47 chromosomes (one extra), not 45 (which would represent a monosomy, the opposite abnormality).
distractorNotes.C: Chromosome 21 is an autosome, not a sex chromosome, so Down syndrome is not a sex chromosome aberration.

questions.stem: During excitation contraction coupling of carciac myocyte, which of _ the following occurs?

options.A: Calcium entering the cell is immediately pumped by Na*-Ca”* exchanger
options.C: The sarcoplasmic Ca”* uptake is important for the myocyte contraction
options.D: Relaxation is inhibited by myocardial ischemia due to accumulation of

questions.subject: Physiology

editorialExplanation.explanation: Myocardial ischemia depletes ATP, impairing the energy-dependent SERCA pump's ability to remove calcium from the cytoplasm back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum, causing intracellular calcium (and often hydrogen ions from anaerobic metabolism) to accumulate and directly interfere with normal relaxation -- a well-established mechanism underlying the diastolic dysfunction seen in ischemic myocardium. This is a genuine, correctly-described pathophysiological consequence, in contrast to calcium being 'immediately' extruded by the Na+-Ca2+ exchanger upon cell entry (the exchanger's extrusion role is more prominent during relaxation, after contraction, not immediately upon calcium's arrival), and in contrast to ryanodine receptors being inhibited during excitation-contraction coupling, when in fact they are actively opened/activated to release stored calcium.

distractorNotes.A: Calcium entering during depolarization first triggers calcium-induced calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, driving contraction; the Na+-Ca2+ exchanger's role in extruding calcium out of the cell is more prominent during relaxation, not immediately upon entry.
distractorNotes.B: Ryanodine receptors are ACTIVATED (opened), not inhibited, during excitation-contraction coupling, releasing calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum in response to the trigger calcium signal.
distractorNotes.C: Sarcoplasmic calcium uptake (via SERCA) is primarily associated with relaxation and replenishing SR calcium stores for the next beat, rather than being the direct trigger for the current contraction, which instead depends on calcium release, not uptake.

questions.stem: During isovolumetric ventricular contraction ‘a. Rapid filling of ventricles occur

options.B: The first heart sound is produced
options.C: The maximum volume of blood is ejected
options.D: The tension is decreased while the volume is constant

questions.subject: Physiology

editorialExplanation.explanation: The first heart sound (S1), caused by the closure of the atrioventricular valves, marks the very onset of isovolumetric ventricular contraction, as rising ventricular pressure first exceeds atrial pressure and slams the mitral and tricuspid valves shut. During this brief phase, all four cardiac valves remain closed and ventricular volume stays constant by definition ('isovolumetric'), while intraventricular pressure rises steeply -- meaning no filling occurs, no blood is ejected yet, and tension/pressure is INCREASING rather than decreasing.

distractorNotes.A: Rapid ventricular filling occurs during early diastole, after the AV valves open, not during isovolumetric contraction (a systolic phase where all valves are closed).
distractorNotes.C: Maximum ejection occurs later, once the semilunar valves have opened, not during isovolumetric contraction, when no blood is yet being ejected (volume is constant).
distractorNotes.D: Tension/pressure actually INCREASES, not decreases, during isovolumetric contraction, as the ventricle builds pressure against closed valves at constant volume.

editorialExplanation.explanation: During cardiac embryogenesis the sinus venosus has paired horns; as venous return is progressively redirected to the right side of the developing heart, the left horn regresses and its remnant becomes the coronary sinus (with its most proximal part forming the oblique vein of the left atrium, the vein of Marshall). This is the mirror-image event to the right horn, which instead enlarges and is incorporated into the right atrium as the smooth-walled sinus venarum. The takeaway is a left-right asymmetry rule worth memorising: right sinus horn becomes part of the right atrium; left sinus horn becomes the coronary sinus.

distractorNotes.B: The superior vena cava forms from the right common cardinal vein and right anterior cardinal vein, not the left sinus horn.
distractorNotes.C: The inferior vena cava's hepatic segment forms from the right vitelline vein, unrelated to the left sinus horn.
distractorNotes.D: The crista terminalis is a right atrial ridge marking the junction of the sinus venarum and the primitive atrium, a right-sided derivative, not a left-horn one.

questions.stem: During the isometric contraction pnase of cardiac cycle, what happens to the ventricular volume?

options.D: Decreases as the intraventricular pressure increases

questions.subject: Physiology

editorialExplanation.explanation: By definition, the isometric (isovolumetric) contraction phase is the period during which ventricular volume remains completely unchanged, because all four cardiac valves are closed -- the AV valves have just shut (producing S1) and the semilunar valves have not yet opened -- so no blood can enter or leave the ventricle even as intraventricular pressure rises steeply due to ongoing myocardial contraction. This constant-volume, rising-pressure combination is exactly analogous to isometric (constant-length) contraction in skeletal muscle physiology, which is where this phase gets its name.

distractorNotes.A: Ventricular volume does not decrease during this phase; it remains constant, since all valves are closed and no blood can be ejected yet.
distractorNotes.B: Ventricular volume does not increase during this phase either; it remains constant, since the AV valves have already closed, preventing further filling.
distractorNotes.D: Volume does not decrease at all during this phase; only intraventricular pressure increases while volume stays constant, which is the entire defining feature of the isovolumetric phase.

questions.stem: During which of the foliowing would the intra-pleura! pressure be greater than atmospheric pressure?

options.C: Forced inspiration with the glottis closed
options.D: Forced expiration with the glottis closed

questions.subject: Anatomy

editorialExplanation.explanation: Forced expiration against a closed glottis is the Valsalva manoeuvre: the expiratory muscles actively try to compress the thorax and expel air, but with the glottis sealed, no air can actually leave, so the generated pressure has nowhere to go except to build up within the thorax, driving intrapleural pressure well above atmospheric pressure. This is the one scenario among the options where intrapleural pressure genuinely becomes positive, in contrast to every phase of normal breathing (and even the mirror-image Müller manoeuvre, forced inspiration against a closed glottis, which instead drives intrapleural pressure to an extremely negative value). The physiological takeaway is to pair 'forced expiration, closed glottis' specifically with positive intrapleural/intrathoracic pressure (Valsalva), and 'forced inspiration, closed glottis' with maximally negative intrapleural pressure (Müller).

distractorNotes.A: Active (normal) inspiration makes intrapleural pressure more negative than at rest, not positive.
distractorNotes.B: Passive expiration allows intrapleural pressure to become less negative, approaching but still remaining below atmospheric pressure under normal quiet breathing.
distractorNotes.C: Forced inspiration against a closed glottis (the Müller manoeuvre) drives intrapleural pressure to an extremely negative value, the opposite of positive.

questions.stem: Elastic cartilage provides structural support for the respiratory airway: ‏ا‎ ‎a. Trachea b. Bronchi 7
questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: Within the respiratory airway, elastic cartilage is specifically found in parts of the larynx -- the epiglottis, and the corniculate and cuneiform cartilages -- in contrast to the trachea and bronchi, whose supporting cartilage rings are entirely hyaline cartilage, and the bronchioles, which have no cartilage support at all (a defining feature distinguishing them from bronchi). While the larynx as a whole is actually a mix of hyaline (thyroid and cricoid cartilages, most of the arytenoids) and elastic (epiglottis, corniculate, cuneiform) cartilage types, it is the only one of the four listed airway structures that contains any elastic cartilage at all, making it the best answer among the options given.

distractorNotes.A: The trachea's supporting C-shaped rings are entirely hyaline cartilage, not elastic cartilage.
distractorNotes.B: The bronchi's supporting cartilage plates are entirely hyaline cartilage, not elastic cartilage.
distractorNotes.C: Bronchioles have no cartilage support at all, elastic or hyaline -- the loss of cartilage is precisely what defines the transition from bronchus to bronchiole.

questions.stem: Eleventh. 1 @)-Regarding the external - intercostal: muscle; indicate the wrong: statement: mo

options.A: It is most superficially placed muscle of the intercostal space
options.B: Its fibers are directed downward and forward
options.D: It extends from the rib tubercle to the costochondral junction
options.C: All posterior intercostal arteries are branches from descending thoracic

questions.subject: Anatomy

editorialExplanation.explanation: Claiming that ALL posterior intercostal arteries arise from the descending thoracic aorta overlooks the well-established exception for the first two intercostal spaces, whose posterior intercostal arteries instead arise from the superior (supreme) intercostal artery, a branch of the costocervical trunk off the subclavian artery -- making the word 'all' the specific overreach that turns this into the false statement. The remaining three statements correctly describe the external intercostal muscle itself: it is the most superficially placed of the three intercostal muscle layers, its fibres run obliquely downward and forward, and it extends from the rib tubercle posteriorly to the costochondral junction anteriorly. The exam takeaway is to watch for absolute words like 'all' in anatomy statements, since a single well-known exception (here, spaces 1-2's arterial supply) is often exactly what such questions are testing.

distractorNotes.A: True: the external intercostal muscle is the outermost (most superficial) of the three intercostal muscle layers.
distractorNotes.B: True: its fibres run obliquely downward and forward, from the rib above to the rib below.
distractorNotes.D: True: it spans from the tubercle of the rib above to the costochondral junction, continuing anteriorly as the anterior intercostal membrane.

questions.subject: Physiology

editorialExplanation.explanation: Oxygen tension (arterial PO2), not oxygen content, is the most potent stimulus specifically detected by the peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid and aortic bodies), which is precisely why these receptors respond powerfully to hypoxic hypoxia (low PO2, as at altitude) but are essentially blind to anaemia or carbon monoxide poisoning, where oxygen content falls while PO2 itself remains normal. This PO2-specific sensitivity is a defining, frequently tested distinguishing feature of the peripheral chemoreceptors compared with the central chemoreceptors, which instead respond primarily to CO2/H+ rather than oxygen levels at all.

questions.stem: Hassall's corpuscles in thymus are characterized by:

options.C: Formed of large number of active lymphocytes

questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: Hassall's corpuscles are a defining histological feature specifically of the thymic medulla, appearing as concentrically arranged, keratinizing epithelial reticular cells forming whorled, eosinophilic (not basophilic) structures. Rather than decreasing with age, Hassall's corpuscles actually tend to become more numerous and prominent as the thymus involutes with age, even as the overall lymphoid (thymocyte) content of the gland declines -- and they are composed of degenerating epithelial cells, not lymphocytes, which are simply interspersed around them in the surrounding medullary tissue.

distractorNotes.A: Hassall's corpuscles are eosinophilic (acidophilic), not basophilic, owing to their keratin content.
distractorNotes.C: Hassall's corpuscles are formed of degenerating, keratinizing epithelial reticular cells, not lymphocytes.
distractorNotes.D: Hassall's corpuscles increase, rather than decrease, in number and prominence with age, even as the thymus otherwise involutes.

questions.stem: have peripheral dark small lymph with germinal center that have large B-lymph, low T-lymph
Heart failure cells are

options.B: Found in the lining of bronchi

questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: 'Heart failure cells' are haemosiderin-laden alveolar macrophages that accumulate in the lungs during chronic pulmonary venous congestion (classically from left-sided heart failure or mitral stenosis), having phagocytosed red blood cells and haemoglobin breakdown products that leaked into the alveolar spaces from congested pulmonary capillaries. Being macrophages, they can be specifically identified and demonstrated using vital (supravital) staining techniques, the same general principle used to identify mononuclear phagocytic system cells elsewhere in the body, and their haemosiderin content classically stains with Prussian blue (Perls') stain. They are free cells within the alveolar lumen rather than a lining cell type, are not ciliated, and are round-to-oval macrophages rather than flat cells, which instead describes the alveolar (Type I pneumocyte) lining itself.

distractorNotes.A: Heart failure cells are macrophages, not ciliated epithelial cells.
distractorNotes.B: Heart failure cells are found as free cells within the alveolar lumen, not lining the bronchi.
distractorNotes.C: Flat cells with flat nuclei describes the thin, squamous Type I pneumocytes forming the alveolar lining, not the round-to-oval macrophages that constitute heart failure cells.

questions.stem: Hypertension develops when the: “a. Amount of collagen fibers in media of arterioles becomes high

options.A: Amount of collagen fibers in media of arterioles becomes high.
options.B: Amount of elastic fibers in media of arterioles becomes low.
options.C: Tone of smooth muscles in media of arterioles becomes high.

questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: The most direct, physiologically fundamental mechanism of hypertension is an increase in arteriolar smooth muscle tone, which raises total peripheral resistance -- since arterial blood pressure equals cardiac output multiplied by total peripheral resistance, a sustained increase in arteriolar tone directly and immediately elevates blood pressure. This mechanism, mediated by increased sympathetic vasoconstrictor activity or other vasoconstrictor influences on arteriolar smooth muscle, is the standard, most emphasized cause taught for essential (primary) hypertension. Increased collagen deposition or adventitial thickening are instead chronic structural remodelling changes that can result FROM sustained hypertension, rather than being the primary, direct trigger of the pressure elevation itself.

distractorNotes.A: Increased collagen in the arteriolar media is more a chronic structural consequence of long-standing hypertension (vascular remodelling/stiffening) than its direct, primary cause.
distractorNotes.B: A decrease in elastic fibres would reduce arteriolar compliance over time, but this is a slower structural change, not the immediate, primary mechanism raising peripheral resistance.
distractorNotes.D: Increased adventitial thickness is a structural remodelling change, not the direct, acute mechanism by which peripheral resistance and blood pressure rise.

editorialExplanation.explanation: The root of the right lung's standard posterior relations include the azygos vein (arching over it to reach the SVC) and the oesophagus, not the inferior vena cava -- the IVC passes directly into the right atrium at the diaphragm's caval opening (T8) and is not a structure conventionally described as lying anterior or posterior to the lung root at the T5-T7 level, making this claim the incorrect one the question is looking for. The other statements are standard true facts about the lung root: it lies opposite the bodies of T5, T6, and T7 vertebrae, it contains the bronchial vessels supplying nutrition to the lung tissue, and the left lung root does have the descending thoracic aorta running posterior to it (so the root correctly sits anterior to the aorta). The exam takeaway is to keep the right lung root's true posterior neighbours (azygos vein, oesophagus) distinct from the IVC, which belongs to a different, lower diaphragmatic level.

distractorNotes.A: True: the root of the lung on both sides lies opposite the bodies of the fifth, sixth, and seventh thoracic vertebrae.
distractorNotes.B: True: the bronchial arteries and veins, supplying nutrition to lung tissue, are genuine contents of the lung root alongside the bronchus, pulmonary vessels, nerves, and lymphatics.
distractorNotes.D: True: the descending thoracic aorta runs posterior to the root of the left lung, so from the root's perspective it correctly sits anterior to the aorta.

questions.stem: If the lungs experimentally filled completely with saline, so the surface tension of fluid lining alveoli is:

options.A: Increased slightly with increase lung compliance
options.C: Remains constant with no change in lung compliance
options.D: Completely lost with increase in lung compliance

questions.subject: Anatomy

editorialExplanation.explanation: This is the classic saline-filled-lung experiment demonstrating that surface tension, not tissue elasticity, is the dominant source of the lung's elastic recoil under normal air-filled conditions: filling the alveoli completely with saline eliminates the air-liquid interface entirely (both surfaces of the alveolar lining fluid are now liquid-liquid), so surface tension's contribution to recoil is essentially abolished. With surface tension removed, the pressure needed to inflate the lung drops dramatically, meaning lung compliance rises sharply -- saline-filled lungs are far easier to inflate than air-filled ones at the same pressures. The physiological takeaway is that this experiment is the classic proof that surfactant's job is specifically to reduce the air-liquid interface's surface tension, since removing that interface altogether reproduces the same easy-inflation effect surfactant partially achieves.

distractorNotes.A: Surface tension is essentially eliminated, not merely 'increased slightly', when the air-liquid interface is removed by saline filling.
distractorNotes.C: Compliance changes dramatically (increases) in this experiment; it does not remain constant, since removing the air-liquid interface removes a major component of the lung's normal elastic recoil.

Ifa parent is a carrier of a chromosome 21 translocation, he might have a child with:
questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: A parent who is a balanced carrier of a Robertsonian translocation involving chromosome 21 (commonly a t(14;21) translocation) carries the correct total amount of chromosome 21 genetic material, just rearranged, and is phenotypically normal -- but during meiosis, this carrier can pass on an unbalanced combination to a child, resulting in effectively three functional copies of chromosome 21 material despite a total chromosome count that may appear as 46 (translocation-type Down syndrome), producing the Down syndrome phenotype. This is the classic mechanism behind 'familial' or translocation Down syndrome, distinct from the more common sporadic trisomy 21 caused by meiotic non-disjunction. The exam takeaway is to associate a parental chromosome 21 translocation carrier state specifically with an increased recurrence risk of having a child with Down syndrome.

distractorNotes.A: Turner's syndrome results from monosomy of the X chromosome, unrelated to a chromosome 21 translocation.
distractorNotes.C: Klinefelter's syndrome results from an extra X chromosome (47,XXY), unrelated to a chromosome 21 translocation.
distractorNotes.D: Chronic myeloid leukaemia results from a reciprocal translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22 (the Philadelphia chromosome), an entirely different translocation from one involving chromosome 21.

questions.stem: In a resting adult, what's the normal ventricular ejection fraction?
questions.subject: Physiology

editorialExplanation.explanation: The normal resting ventricular ejection fraction in a healthy adult is typically cited as approximately 55% to 70%, representing the proportion of end-diastolic ventricular volume that is ejected with each systolic contraction under normal conditions. Values below this normal range (particularly below 40%) are used clinically to define reduced ejection fraction and systolic heart failure, making 55% the standard lower-limit-of-normal figure most frequently cited in physiology teaching among the given options.

distractorNotes.A: 20% is far below even the pathologically reduced range seen in severe heart failure, not a normal resting value.
distractorNotes.B: 30% falls well within the pathologically reduced ejection fraction range associated with heart failure, not a normal resting value.
distractorNotes.C: 40% is at the threshold typically used to define reduced ejection fraction heart failure, not a normal resting value.

questions.stem: In an ECG recording, the time between atria! depolarization & ventricular depolarization is represented by which part?
questions.subject: Physiology

editorialExplanation.explanation: The P-R segment is the isoelectric portion of the ECG tracing specifically spanning the gap between the end of atrial depolarization (end of the P wave) and the start of ventricular depolarization (beginning of the QRS complex) -- this flat segment represents the physiological delay imposed by slow conduction through the AV node, allowing the atria to finish contracting before the ventricles are activated. This is distinct from the P-R INTERVAL, which additionally includes the P wave itself (measuring from the start of atrial depolarization rather than its end).

distractorNotes.A: The P-wave itself represents atrial depolarization, not the gap/interval between atrial and ventricular depolarization.
distractorNotes.B: The QRS complex represents ventricular depolarization itself, not the preceding gap between atrial and ventricular depolarization.
distractorNotes.C: The S-T interval represents the period between the end of ventricular depolarization and the start of ventricular repolarization, unrelated to the atrial-to-ventricular depolarization gap.

questions.stem: In bronchiole, cell degrades the toxin in inhaled air is: !
questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: Clara (club) cells, the non-ciliated secretory cells of the bronchiolar epithelium, are rich in smooth endoplasmic reticulum and cytochrome P450 enzymes, giving them a well-established detoxification role -- metabolising and neutralising inhaled toxins, xenobiotics, and pollutants that reach the smaller conducting airways. This detoxifying function is one of Clara cells' several distinct roles, alongside secreting a protective surfactant-like fluid and serving as progenitor (stem) cells for bronchiolar epithelial regeneration.

distractorNotes.B: Basal cells serve as a progenitor cell population for the epithelium in larger airways (trachea, bronchi) but are not specifically known for toxin detoxification.
distractorNotes.D: Goblet cells secrete mucus for trapping inhaled particles, a mechanical protective role, not enzymatic toxin detoxification.

questions.stem: In hypovolemis shock, which of the following receptors are stimulated?

options.A: Baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch
options.B: Peripheral chemoreceptors in the aortic and carotid bodies

questions.subject: Physiology

editorialExplanation.explanation: In hypovolaemic shock, the arterial baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch are the primary sensors engaged by the fall in blood pressure and stretch, triggering the baroreceptor reflex arc that reduces vagal tone and increases sympathetic outflow -- producing the compensatory tachycardia, vasoconstriction, and increased contractility characteristic of the body's initial response to blood loss. While technically the baroreceptors' firing rate DECREASES as pressure falls (since they are stretch receptors), this baroreceptor reflex arc is the standard, most emphasized primary compensatory mechanism engaged in hypovolaemic shock, distinguishing it from the peripheral and central chemoreceptor pathways, which become significantly engaged only with more severe, decompensated hypoxaemia or acidaemia.

distractorNotes.B: Peripheral chemoreceptors respond primarily to hypoxaemia and become significantly activated only in more severe, decompensated shock, not as the primary initial hypovolaemic shock response.
distractorNotes.C: Atrial (low-pressure) stretch receptors do respond to reduced venous filling as a secondary/complementary reflex arc, but the arterial baroreceptor reflex is the primary, most classically emphasized mechanism.
distractorNotes.D: Central chemoreceptors respond to CSF pH/CO2 changes, not directly activated by hypovolaemia itself.

questions.stem: In progressive hemorrhagic shock, which of the following occurs? ~~’
questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: As hemorrhagic shock progresses from its compensated toward its decompensated (progressive) stage, prolonged tissue hypoperfusion and hypoxia trigger the release of inflammatory mediators and metabolic byproducts that damage capillary endothelium, increasing capillary permeability -- this allows fluid and even plasma proteins to leak out of the vascular space into the interstitium, further reducing effective circulating blood volume and creating a vicious, self-worsening cycle that is the hallmark of the 'progressive' (as opposed to compensated) phase of shock. This mechanism is part of why hemorrhagic shock can become progressively harder to reverse the longer it continues, even after the initial bleeding is controlled. The exam takeaway is to associate increased capillary permeability specifically with the transition from compensated to progressive/decompensated shock.

distractorNotes.B: The compensatory response to hemorrhage is widespread venoconstriction (to maintain venous return and cardiac filling from the reduced blood volume), not venous dilation, at least until very late, irreversible decompensation.
distractorNotes.C: Progressive shock produces tissue hypoxia and anaerobic metabolism, leading to lactic ACIDOSIS, not alkalosis -- the opposite of what this option states.
distractorNotes.D: Renal hypoperfusion and compensatory fluid conservation in shock lead to DECREASED, not increased, urine output (oliguria).

questions.stem: In the interphase of cell cycle, synthesis (S) phase shows:

options.A: Cells grow in size and acquire ATP

questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: Centriole duplication occurs specifically during the S (synthesis) phase of interphase, running in parallel with DNA replication, so that by the time the cell cycle proceeds through G2 and into mitosis, each future daughter cell will inherit a complete, duplicated centrosome ready to organise its own spindle apparatus. This precise timing (centrioles and DNA both duplicating during S phase) is a specific, frequently tested cell-cycle fact, distinguishing S phase's defining events from the general cell growth of G1/G2 (option A) or the tubulin/spindle assembly activity more associated with the G2-to-M transition (option D).

distractorNotes.A: General cell growth and ATP/energy accumulation are characteristic of the G1 and G2 growth phases surrounding S phase, not S phase's own defining event.
distractorNotes.B: Describing the nucleus as containing '46 single chromosomes (chromatids)' describes the pre-replication (G1) state, before S phase has duplicated the DNA into sister chromatid pairs.
distractorNotes.D: Tubulin synthesis in preparation for spindle formation is more specifically associated with the G2 phase, immediately preceding mitosis, rather than S phase itself.

questions.stem: In the sinoatrial (SA) node, phase 4 depolarization (pacemaker potential) isattributable to
questions.subject: Physiology

editorialExplanation.explanation: The pacemaker (phase 4) depolarization of the SA node is driven substantially by the 'funny current' (If), a mixed cation current carried significantly by an increasing Na+ conductance that activates upon repolarization/hyperpolarization and slowly depolarizes the cell toward threshold. This progressive rise in inward Na+ current, together with a declining outward K+ current and, later, activation of T-type and L-type calcium channels, together produce the characteristic slow, unstable diastolic depolarization unique to pacemaker tissue.

distractorNotes.A: Phase 4 depolarization is driven by a DECREASE, not an increase, in K+ conductance as the delayed rectifier K+ channels progressively close.
distractorNotes.C: A decrease in chloride conductance is not an established, primary mechanism of SA node phase 4 depolarization.

questions.stem: In the sinoatrial (SA) node, phase 4 depolarization (pacemaker potential) is attributable to
questions.subject: Physiology

editorialExplanation.explanation: This is a duplicate of the sibling question; the pacemaker potential (phase 4) is substantially driven by the funny current's increasing Na+ conductance, contributing to the slow, spontaneous depolarization characteristic of SA node pacemaker cells.

distractorNotes.A: Phase 4 involves a decrease, not increase, in K+ conductance.
distractorNotes.C: Decreased chloride conductance is not an established primary mechanism here.
distractorNotes.D: Calcium conductance actually INCREASES (via T-type and later L-type channels), not decreases, contributing to the later part of phase 4 depolarization.

questions.stem: In the spleen, white pulp:

options.A: Is formed of cords and sinuses
options.C: Is lymphatic nodule with central arteriole

questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: The spleen's white pulp is fundamentally a lymphoid nodule (follicle) organised concentrically around a central arteriole, forming the spleen's immune-surveillance compartment analogous to a lymph node's cortex, in contrast to the red pulp's blood-filtering role. This central arteriole, an eccentrically-positioned branch of the splenic artery, is the defining anatomical landmark used to identify white pulp under the microscope, distinguishing it from the cords-and-sinusoids architecture and abundant red blood cells that instead characterise the red pulp, and from the four (not two) zones that make up the complete white pulp structure (PALS, germinal centre, follicular/mantle zone, and marginal zone).

distractorNotes.A: Cords (Billroth cords) and sinusoids are the defining architecture of the red pulp, not the white pulp.
distractorNotes.B: An abundance of red blood cells is characteristic of the red pulp, which filters blood, not the lymphoid-tissue-dominated white pulp.
distractorNotes.D: White pulp is conventionally described as having four zones (periarteriolar lymphatic sheath, germinal centre, follicular/mantle zone, and marginal zone), not only two.

questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: In the aorta and other large elastic arteries, the tunica media is packed with 40 to 70 concentric, fenestrated elastic laminae that dominate the entire wall thickness, making the specific internal elastic lamina (the single boundary lamina that clearly demarcates intima from media in muscular arteries) impossible to distinguish as a separate, distinct structure from the many other elastic laminae surrounding it. This is in sharp contrast to muscular (medium-sized) arteries, where the media is dominated by smooth muscle rather than elastic laminae, allowing the single internal elastic lamina to stand out clearly as a well-defined, wavy line under the microscope. The histology takeaway is that the internal elastic lamina's visibility as a distinct boundary depends on it contrasting against a media that is NOT itself full of elastic tissue -- a contrast that elastic arteries like the aorta lack.

distractorNotes.A: The internal elastic lamina is present in the aorta's wall, just not distinguishable as a separate structure from the surrounding elastic laminae, rather than being entirely absent.
distractorNotes.B: The issue is not the lamina's thinness but that it cannot be told apart from the many other, equally prominent elastic laminae filling the media.
distractorNotes.D: The internal elastic lamina, like the aorta's other elastic laminae, does take up elastic stains; the issue is distinguishing it as a separate structure, not a staining failure.

questions.stem: Increases in which of the following variables would be expected to decrease the venous return?
variants: [EOM 196 104 2023 No answers  (1).pdf p9 #63] Increases in which of the following variables would be expected to decrease the venous return? :: A) Cardiac output D) Venous resistance
questions.subject: Physiology

editorialExplanation.explanation: Venous return is governed by the pressure gradient driving blood back to the heart divided by the resistance to that venous flow, so increasing the vascular resistance to venous blood directly decreases venous return by increasing the denominator of this relationship, for any given driving pressure. This contrasts with increases in cardiac output, mean systemic filling pressure, or blood volume, all of which tend to INCREASE venous return -- cardiac output by lowering right atrial pressure and widening the pressure gradient, and mean systemic filling pressure/blood volume by directly raising the driving pressure for venous return.

distractorNotes.B: Increased cardiac output tends to increase venous return, by pumping blood forward more effectively and lowering right atrial pressure, widening the gradient driving venous return.
distractorNotes.C: Increased mean systemic filling pressure directly increases the driving pressure for venous return, increasing (not decreasing) it.
distractorNotes.D: Increased blood volume generally raises mean systemic filling pressure, thereby increasing (not decreasing) venous return.

options.B: Shift the length tension relationship up and left
options.D: Decrease in degree of shortening of myocytes Page 2 of

questions.subject: Physiology

editorialExplanation.explanation: Increasing the heart's inotropic state (contractility) shifts the length-tension relationship upward and to the left on a standard plot, meaning more active tension is generated at any given sarcomere length (and even at a somewhat shorter length than before), reflecting enhanced calcium handling and cross-bridge cycling independent of any change in preload. This is distinct from the force-velocity relationship, which shifts UP and to the right (not down) with increased inotropy, with Vmax (velocity at zero load) genuinely INCREASING rather than staying unchanged, and with the overall degree of myocardial shortening increasing rather than decreasing.

distractorNotes.A: Increased inotropy shifts the force-velocity relationship UP and to the right, not down, reflecting greater force and velocity capacity at any given load.
distractorNotes.C: Vmax, the velocity of shortening at zero load, genuinely INCREASES with increased inotropy -- it is a classic, load-independent index of enhanced contractility, not an unchanged parameter.
distractorNotes.D: Increased inotropy INCREASES, not decreases, the degree of myocyte shortening at any given preload and afterload.

questions.stem: Internal elastic lamina is developed in the tunica intima of:
questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: The internal elastic lamina is a well-defined, wavy sheet of elastic tissue marking the boundary between the tunica intima and tunica media, and it is most clearly and consistently developed in arteries, particularly muscular (medium-sized) arteries where it stands out sharply against the smooth-muscle-dominated media. Veins generally lack a well-developed internal elastic lamina, and capillaries and lymphatic vessels are far too simple in construction (essentially just endothelium and minimal surrounding connective tissue) to have distinct tunica layers or an internal elastic lamina at all. The histology takeaway is to associate a prominent internal elastic lamina specifically with the arterial side of the circulation, most classically taught using muscular arteries as the example.

distractorNotes.B: Veins characteristically lack a well-developed internal elastic lamina, unlike arteries.
distractorNotes.C: Capillaries have only a single endothelial layer and lack the distinct tunica layers (including any elastic lamina) that define larger vessels.
distractorNotes.D: Lymphatic vessels, like capillaries, are simple-walled and lack a distinct internal elastic lamina.

questions.stem: Klinefelter’s syndrome is:
questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: Klinefelter syndrome patients (47,XXY), despite being genetically and phenotypically male, are Barr-body positive -- they show one Barr body in their cell nuclei, just like a normal female, because the presence of a second X chromosome results in one X being inactivated regardless of the overall karyotype. This unusual sex-chromatin positivity in an otherwise male individual is one of the most classic and frequently tested distinguishing laboratory features of Klinefelter syndrome, historically used as a simple screening clue before karyotyping became routine.

distractorNotes.A: 45,XO (Turner syndrome) is an unrelated karyotype describing a different condition (monosomy X), not Klinefelter syndrome.
distractorNotes.B: Klinefelter syndrome's karyotype totals 47 chromosomes (47,XXY), not 46 -- 46,XXY would be numerically inconsistent, since three sex chromosomes plus 44 autosomes total 47, not 46.

questions.stem: Lack of surfactant produces all of the above EXCEPT:

options.A: Collapse of small alveoli and expansion of large alveoli

questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: Surfactant deficiency (as in neonatal respiratory distress syndrome) directly and classically causes increased alveolar surface tension, leading to instability and collapse of smaller alveoli (with relatively over-distended larger ones, per Laplace's law), decreased lung compliance (stiffer lungs requiring more pressure to inflate), and consequently increased work of breathing to achieve adequate ventilation. Total lung capacity, however, is a maximal structural lung volume measurement that is not as directly or primarily affected by surfactant deficiency as compliance and functional residual capacity are -- TLC reduction is a less specific, less directly emphasized consequence of surfactant deficiency compared with the other three classic, textbook pathophysiological effects.

distractorNotes.A: Collapse of small alveoli with relative overexpansion of larger ones is a direct, classic consequence of increased surface tension from surfactant deficiency (unstable alveoli per Laplace's law).
distractorNotes.B: Decreased lung compliance is a direct, defining consequence of increased alveolar surface tension from surfactant deficiency.
distractorNotes.D: Increased work of breathing directly follows from decreased lung compliance, both classic consequences of surfactant deficiency.

questions.stem: Large elastic arteries are characterized by:

options.A: Longitudinal smooth muscles in tunica adventitia. |

variants: [EOY 104 FINALS (answered) (1) (1).pdf p27 #12] Large elastic arteries are characterized by: :: A) Longitudinal smooth muscles in tunica adventitia B) Valves in their walls D) Prominent external elastic lamina (EEL)
questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: Large elastic arteries like the aorta are histologically defined by their tunica media containing 40 to 70 concentric, fenestrated elastic laminae (membranes), an adaptation that lets the vessel wall stretch during systole and recoil during diastole, smoothing out the pulsatile flow from the heart into a steadier downstream flow (the Windkessel effect). This is THE hallmark, most frequently tested feature distinguishing elastic arteries from muscular (medium) arteries, whose media is instead dominated by smooth muscle with only a modest number of elastic laminae. The exam takeaway is to fix this specific number range (40-70 elastic membranes) as the signature identifying feature of elastic arteries on a histology slide.

distractorNotes.A: Longitudinal smooth muscle bundles can be found in the tunica adventitia of large elastic arteries, a real but secondary, less emphasized feature compared to the defining elastic laminae of the media.
distractorNotes.B: Valves are a feature of veins (particularly medium-sized limb veins), not arteries.
distractorNotes.D: A single, prominent, distinctly identifiable external elastic lamina is a feature more associated with muscular arteries; in elastic arteries, the media's many elastic laminae make any single lamina, internal or external, hard to distinguish separately.

questions.stem: large laryngeal Cartilage is characterized by All except
Less developed spirally arranged smooth muscles are a feature of:
questions.subject: Anatomy

editorialExplanation.explanation: In the trachea and extrapulmonary bronchi, smooth muscle is confined to the posterior wall as the trachealis muscle, bridging the open ends of the C-shaped cartilage rings -- a comparatively rudimentary, incomplete arrangement compared with what develops further down the airway tree. As the airways branch into intrapulmonary bronchi and then bronchioles, cartilage support progressively disappears and the smooth muscle instead forms a well-developed, continuous spiral (helical) layer encircling the full airway wall, which is what allows bronchioles to actively regulate their calibre (bronchoconstriction/dilation). The histology takeaway is to associate the trachea with minimal, posteriorly-restricted smooth muscle and to associate bronchioles with the airway's most developed circumferential smooth muscle layer.

distractorNotes.A: Intrapulmonary bronchi already show a more developed, more completely circumferential spiral smooth muscle arrangement than the trachea, as cartilage support becomes discontinuous plates rather than complete rings.
distractorNotes.B: Bronchioles have the most developed, complete spiral smooth muscle layer in the airway tree, the opposite extreme from 'less developed'.
distractorNotes.C: Alveolar sacs and ducts have only minimal smooth muscle (small muscular 'knobs' at alveolar mouths) rather than an organised spiral arrangement at all, so 'less developed spiral muscle' does not describe them either.

questions.stem: Longitudinal splitting of chromosomes happens in the following phase:
questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: Anaphase is defined by the longitudinal splitting of each chromosome's centromere, separating the two sister chromatids so that each is pulled by shortening kinetochore microtubules toward opposite poles of the dividing cell. This is the precise moment the genetic material is physically divided into two equal sets, immediately preceding telophase, when the cell begins to re-form two separate nuclei around each set of chromosomes. The exam takeaway is to fix 'centromere/chromosome splits, sister chromatids separate' as anaphase's single defining event, distinguishing it from prophase (chromosome condensation), metaphase (alignment at the equator), and telophase (nuclear reformation).

distractorNotes.A: Prophase is characterised by chromosome condensation and spindle formation, not chromatid separation.
distractorNotes.B: Metaphase is characterised by chromosomes aligning at the cell's equatorial plate, held intact (not yet split) by spindle fibres from both poles.
distractorNotes.D: Telophase is characterised by nuclear envelope reformation and chromosome decondensation around the already-separated chromatid sets, occurring after the splitting event of anaphase.

questions.stem: Low resistance shock is characterized by which of the following?

options.A: Occurs when the size of the vascular system is increased by
options.B: associated with an increase of the venous return
options.C: Skin is cold and pale in septic shock
options.D: Is characterized by decreased blood volume

questions.subject: Physiology

editorialExplanation.explanation: Low-resistance (distributive) shock, such as septic, anaphylactic, or neurogenic shock, occurs when widespread loss of vasomotor tone effectively increases the size (capacitance) of the vascular system beyond what the available blood volume can adequately fill, creating a relative hypovolaemia even without any actual blood loss. This is mechanistically distinct from hypovolaemic shock (an actual reduction in circulating blood volume) and is associated with DECREASED, not increased, effective venous return, since blood pools within the abnormally dilated vascular bed rather than returning efficiently to the heart. Notably, in early ('warm') septic shock specifically, the skin is characteristically warm and flushed rather than cold and pale, since the vasodilation increases skin blood flow -- the opposite of the cold, pale, clammy skin classically seen in hypovolaemic or cardiogenic shock.

distractorNotes.B: Low-resistance/distributive shock is associated with DECREASED effective venous return, as blood pools in the abnormally dilated vasculature, not an increase.
distractorNotes.C: In early ('warm') septic shock, the skin is characteristically warm and flushed due to vasodilation, not cold and pale, which instead describes hypovolaemic or cardiogenic shock.
distractorNotes.D: Decreased blood volume is the defining feature of hypovolaemic shock, not low-resistance/distributive shock, which typically has normal blood volume that is simply maldistributed.

editorialExplanation.explanation: Clara (club) cells are a defining, hallmark feature of the bronchiolar mucosa, appearing as non-ciliated, dome-shaped secretory cells interspersed among the remaining ciliated cells once goblet cells have largely disappeared at this level of the airway. This distinguishes bronchioles both from the goblet-cell-rich epithelium of the trachea and bronchi above them, and from the cartilage-supported walls of bronchi, since bronchioles characteristically lack cartilage plates altogether, relying instead on a well-developed smooth (not striated) muscle coat for their walls.

distractorNotes.C: Airway smooth muscle, including in bronchioles, is smooth muscle, not striated muscle, which is an entirely different tissue type (skeletal/cardiac).

questions.stem: Lung emphysema decreases the pulmonary diffusing capacity for gases due to:

options.A: Decreased the surface area of respiratory membrane

questions.subject: Anatomy

editorialExplanation.explanation: Emphysema is characterised by destruction of alveolar walls and septa, which merges many small alveoli into fewer, larger air spaces and directly reduces the total surface area of the respiratory membrane available for gas exchange. Since diffusing capacity is directly proportional to the surface area available for diffusion (per Fick's law of diffusion), this loss of surface area is the principal mechanism by which emphysema lowers pulmonary diffusing capacity, distinct from diseases like pulmonary fibrosis that instead impair diffusion by thickening the membrane. The exam takeaway is to pair emphysema specifically with reduced SURFACE AREA (destructive disease) and fibrosis/oedema with increased membrane THICKNESS (restrictive/interstitial disease) as the two classic, distinct mechanisms of impaired diffusion.

distractorNotes.B: Increased membrane thickness is the mechanism behind reduced diffusing capacity in interstitial lung diseases like pulmonary fibrosis or pulmonary oedema, not emphysema, which instead destroys tissue and reduces surface area.
distractorNotes.C: Emphysema is characterised by decreased, not increased, elastic recoil of lung tissue, due to elastase-mediated destruction of elastin fibres.
distractorNotes.D: Gas solubility is an intrinsic physicochemical property of the gas and the diffusion medium; it is not altered by emphysema.

questions.stem: May be due to 47 chromosomes (XXY). 15, Structural aberrations include:
questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: Deletion -- the loss of a chromosomal segment -- is a classic structural chromosomal aberration, involving a change to a chromosome's physical structure/composition rather than a change to the overall chromosome count. This distinguishes it from numerical aberrations like aneuploidy (an abnormal chromosome count, such as trisomy or monosomy) and from clinical syndromes such as Turner's or Klinefelter's, which are themselves the phenotypic consequences of numerical (not structural) chromosomal abnormalities rather than being structural aberration categories in themselves. The exam takeaway is to keep the two broad categories distinct: numerical aberrations (aneuploidy, polyploidy) change chromosome count; structural aberrations (deletion, duplication, translocation, inversion, ring chromosome, isochromosome) change chromosome architecture.

distractorNotes.A: Aneuploidy is a numerical chromosomal aberration (an abnormal chromosome count), not a structural one.
distractorNotes.C: Turner's syndrome is a clinical condition resulting from a numerical aberration (monosomy X), not itself a category of structural aberration.
distractorNotes.D: Klinefelter's syndrome is a clinical condition resulting from a numerical aberration (an extra X chromosome), not itself a category of structural aberration.

questions.stem: Medium sized vein is characterized by:

options.A: Its tunica adventitia is thicker than tunica media
options.B: They have internal and external elastic laminae
options.C: Its wall does not collapse after death
options.D: The subendothelium is rich in elastic fibers

questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: A defining histological feature distinguishing veins from arteries is that the tunica adventitia is typically the thickest layer of a vein's wall -- often containing longitudinal smooth muscle bundles -- in clear contrast to arteries, where the tunica media (built for withstanding higher pressure) is the dominant, thickest layer. This reflects the different functional demands: veins operate at low pressure and serve as a capacitance reservoir, needing structural support (adventitia) more than a thick muscular pressure-resisting layer (media). The exam takeaway is to pair 'adventitia thicker than media' specifically with veins, the functional and structural mirror image of arteries.

distractorNotes.B: Veins generally lack well-developed internal and external elastic laminae, a feature instead characteristic of arteries.
distractorNotes.C: It is actually arteries, with their thicker, more elastic and muscular walls, that tend to remain more open (less collapsed) after death; thin-walled veins tend to collapse.
distractorNotes.D: A subendothelium rich in elastic fibres is not a standout, defining feature specifically emphasized for medium veins in standard histology teaching.

Mitosis is characterized by the following: | a. Exchange of genes. | b. Absence of crossing over. | c. Daughier cells contain n chromosomes

options.D: Daughter cells are not identical to mother cells.

questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: Mitosis is characterised by the complete absence of crossing over (and therefore no exchange of genetic material between homologous chromosomes), since it involves no pairing of homologous chromosomes at all -- each chromosome simply duplicates and its sister chromatids separate, producing two daughter cells that are genetically identical to the parent cell and to each other. This is a fundamental distinguishing feature from meiosis, where crossing over during prophase I of the first meiotic division is a defining, essential source of genetic variation among the resulting gametes. The exam takeaway is to pair mitosis strictly with 'no crossing over, genetically identical daughter cells, same (diploid) chromosome number preserved'.

distractorNotes.A: Exchange of genes (crossing over) is a defining feature of meiosis, not mitosis, which involves no pairing of homologous chromosomes.
distractorNotes.C: Mitotic daughter cells retain the same (diploid, 2n) chromosome number as the parent cell, not a haploid (n) number, which is instead the outcome of meiosis.
distractorNotes.D: Mitotic daughter cells are genetically identical to the mother cell (barring rare mutation), not different from it, since no crossing over or independent assortment occurs.

editorialExplanation.explanation: Turner syndrome, karyotype 45,X, results from monosomy of a sex chromosome -- the complete absence of one of the two sex chromosomes normally present, leaving only a single X chromosome and no Y or second X. This is the only human sex chromosome monosomy generally compatible with live birth, in contrast to autosomal monosomies, which are almost always lethal early in development. The exam takeaway is to fix 'Turner syndrome = 45,X = sex chromosome monosomy' as the defining numerical chromosomal fact, distinct from Klinefelter's (sex chromosome trisomy, an extra X) and Down syndrome/Robertsonian translocation (autosomal abnormalities unrelated to sex chromosome count).

distractorNotes.B: Klinefelter's syndrome (47,XXY) is a sex chromosome TRISOMY (an extra chromosome), not a monosomy.
distractorNotes.C: A Robertsonian translocation is a structural rearrangement between two acrocentric chromosomes, not a numerical monosomy of a sex chromosome.
distractorNotes.D: Mongolism (Down syndrome) is caused by trisomy of an autosome (chromosome 21), unrelated to sex chromosome monosomy.
