questions.stem: What's the correct definition of cardiac output?

options.A: Amount of blood delivered through both vena cava per minute
options.B: Amount of blood ejected from a ventricle in each systole times beats per
options.C: Amount of blood ejected from both ventricles in each systole
options.D: Amount of blood ejected frorn the left ventricle in each systole

questions.subject: Anatomy

editorialExplanation.explanation: Cardiac output is formally defined as stroke volume multiplied by heart rate -- the amount of blood ejected by a ventricle in one systole (beat), multiplied by the number of beats per minute -- which is exactly what option B describes ('blood ejected from a ventricle in each systole times beats per [minute]'). This distinguishes cardiac output, a per-minute flow measurement, from stroke volume, which is only the per-beat volume ejected. The exam takeaway is to keep the SV x HR = CO relationship explicit, since distractors in this bank swap 'per systole' language for 'per minute' language to test whether the time unit was understood.

distractorNotes.A: Blood delivered through the venae cavae per minute describes venous return, which equals cardiac output only at haemodynamic steady state -- it is not the definition of cardiac output itself.
distractorNotes.C: This describes a single systole's total ventricular output, missing the essential 'per minute' (heart-rate) component of the true definition.
distractorNotes.D: This describes stroke volume of the left ventricle alone, a per-beat quantity, not cardiac output's per-minute quantity.

questions.stem: What type of tissue forms the alveoli in the lung?
variants: [Histo MCQ by Dr.Kandeel [104].pdf p30 #13] What type of tissue forms the alveoli in the lung? :: A) Simple squamous epithelium B) Stratified squamous epithelium C) Simple columnar epithelium D) Pseudostratified epithelium

[DPT HISTO MCQ [Respiratory].pdf p2 #13] What type of tissue forms the alveoli in the lung? :: A) Simple squamous epithelium B) Simple cuboidal epithelium C) Simple columnar epithelium.d.Pseudostratified epithelium
questions.subject: Anatomy

editorialExplanation.explanation: The alveolar wall is lined by simple squamous epithelium, dominated by thin, flattened Type I pneumocytes that cover roughly 95% of the alveolar surface area, with the remaining surface occupied by the fewer, cuboidal, surfactant-producing Type II pneumocytes. This squamous shape is functionally essential: the extreme thinness of Type I cells minimises the diffusion distance across the alveolar-capillary membrane, which is exactly what efficient passive gas exchange requires. The histology takeaway is to associate simple squamous epithelium specifically with tissues built for rapid diffusion or filtration (alveoli, capillary endothelium, Bowman's capsule's parietal layer), in contrast to cuboidal or columnar epithelium, which favour secretion or absorption.

distractorNotes.B: Simple cuboidal epithelium describes structures built more for secretion or absorption (e.g., kidney tubules, small gland ducts), not the ultra-thin alveolar wall.
distractorNotes.C: Simple columnar epithelium lines absorptive or secretory surfaces like the intestinal lining, far too thick for efficient alveolar gas diffusion.
distractorNotes.D: Pseudostratified (often ciliated) columnar epithelium lines the conducting airways (trachea, bronchi) for mucociliary clearance, not the thin-walled alveoli themselves.

questions.stem: What type of tissues lines the paranasal sinuses: i

options.D: Pseudostratified columnar ciliated epithelium with goblet cells

questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: The paranasal sinuses are lined by a thin pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells, a respiratory-type epithelium continuous with, though thinner and less richly vascularised than, the epithelium lining the nasal cavity proper, with which the sinuses communicate via small ostia. This ciliated, mucus-producing lining allows the sinuses to participate in the same mucociliary clearance system as the rest of the upper respiratory tract, moving mucus and trapped particles out through the sinus openings into the nasal cavity.

distractorNotes.A: Simple squamous epithelium is far too thin and lacks the mucociliary clearance capability needed for the paranasal sinuses.
distractorNotes.B: Simple columnar epithelium without the pseudostratified, ciliated, goblet-cell-rich features does not match the sinus lining's actual respiratory-type structure.
distractorNotes.C: Stratified squamous epithelium, built for mechanical protection against abrasion, is not the epithelium type lining the paranasal sinuses.

questions.stem: What type of tissues lines the paranasalsinuses:

options.D: Rseudostratified columnar cililated epithelium with goblet cells

questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: This is a duplicate of the sibling question; the paranasal sinuses are lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells, the same respiratory-type mucosa continuous with the nasal cavity, supporting mucociliary clearance of the sinus cavities via their ostia into the nose.

distractorNotes.A: Simple squamous epithelium lacks the mucociliary clearance function needed here.
distractorNotes.B: Simple columnar epithelium without pseudostratified, ciliated, goblet-cell features does not match the sinus lining.
distractorNotes.C: Stratified squamous epithelium is not the epithelium type lining the paranasal sinuses.

questions.stem: What would be the change in blood flow to a tissue if radius of the arterioles in that tissue is doubled and perfusion pressure is halved? a, Increase 8 times
questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: By Poiseuille's law, blood flow is directly proportional to the pressure gradient and to the fourth power of the vessel's radius (Flow proportional to Delta-P times r^4). Doubling the radius increases flow by a factor of 2^4 = 16, while halving the perfusion pressure decreases flow by a factor of 2, so the combined effect is 16 multiplied by one-half, giving a net eightfold increase in blood flow. This dramatic radius^4 relationship is precisely why small changes in arteriolar diameter (via smooth muscle tone) have such a powerful effect on local blood flow and total peripheral resistance, far outweighing comparable percentage changes in driving pressure.

distractorNotes.B: A 16-fold increase would result if radius alone were doubled with pressure held constant; it overlooks that halving the pressure cuts this effect in half.
distractorNotes.C: A 4-fold increase does not correctly apply the radius-to-the-fourth-power relationship of Poiseuille's law.
distractorNotes.D: Flow increases rather than decreases overall, since the 16-fold gain from doubling the radius outweighs the 2-fold loss from halving the pressure.

questions.stem: When chromosome divides transversely at centromere, it results in:

options.B: Cells of the mongol child contain 45 chromosomes

variants: [EOY 104 exams Not answerd (1) (1).pdf p15 #9] When chromosome divides transversely at centromere, it results in: | :: A) Duplication B) lsochromosome. | C) Translocation D) Inversion
questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: When a chromosome's centromere divides transversely (across its short axis, perpendicular to the normal longitudinal plane of division) rather than longitudinally, each resulting daughter chromosome ends up with two copies of the same arm instead of one copy of each -- this abnormal event is precisely how an isochromosome is formed, matching this bank's identical, already-established fact from the sibling question on this exact mechanism. This is a distinct structural aberration mechanism from translocation (movement of a segment to a different chromosome) or inversion (a segment reversing orientation within the same chromosome).

distractorNotes.C: Translocation results from an exchange or movement of a segment between chromosomes, an entirely different mechanism from transverse centromere division.
distractorNotes.D: Inversion results from a chromosomal segment reversing its orientation in place, an entirely different mechanism from transverse centromere division.

questions.stem: When the chromosome divides transversely during anaphase:

options.B: It gives rise to Philadelphia chromosome

questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: Normally, a chromosome's centromere splits longitudinally during anaphase, dividing each chromatid so that every daughter cell receives one complete copy of each chromosome arm. If the centromere instead divides transversely (across its short axis, perpendicular to the normal plane of division), each resulting chromosome ends up with two copies of the same arm (either two short arms or two long arms) rather than one of each -- this abnormal event is precisely how an isochromosome is formed. Isochromosomes are a recognised structural chromosomal abnormality with clinical significance, such as the isochromosome of the long arm of the X chromosome (i(Xq)) seen in some cases of Turner syndrome.

distractorNotes.B: The Philadelphia chromosome arises from a reciprocal translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22, an entirely different mechanism from transverse centromere division.
distractorNotes.C: A ring chromosome forms when a chromosome breaks at both ends and the broken ends fuse together, a different mechanism from transverse centromere splitting.
distractorNotes.D: Terminal deletion results from loss of a chromosome's end segment following a single break, not from an abnormal transverse centromere division.

questions.stem: Where do T-lymphocytes acquire their immunocompetence?
variants: [DPT HISTO MCQ [Lymphatic] 2023.pdf p1 #7] Where do T-lymphocytes acquire their immunocompetence? :: A) Thymus. _ B) Thyroid C) Bone marrow D) Lymph node
questions.subject: Anatomy

editorialExplanation.explanation: T-lymphocytes acquire their immunocompetence in the thymus, where bone-marrow-derived precursor cells undergo maturation and rigorous positive and negative selection against self-antigens, ensuring that only functional, self-tolerant T-cells are released to populate the peripheral immune system. This process defines the thymus as a primary (central) lymphoid organ, distinct from secondary (peripheral) lymphoid organs like lymph nodes and the spleen, where already-mature lymphocytes go on to encounter antigen and mount immune responses. The exam takeaway is the clean division of labour: bone marrow makes both B- and T-cell precursors, but only the thymus finishes educating T-cells specifically.

distractorNotes.B: The thyroid is an endocrine gland producing thyroid hormones; it plays no role in lymphocyte maturation.
distractorNotes.C: Bone marrow is where T-cell precursors originate and where B-lymphocytes complete their own maturation, but T-cells specifically require the thymic environment to become immunocompetent.
distractorNotes.D: Lymph nodes are secondary lymphoid organs where mature lymphocytes encounter antigen; they do not mature naive T-cells into immunocompetent cells.

questions.stem: Which cell considered as a part of the phagocytic system:
questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: Littoral cells, the specialised macrophage-derived cells lining the splenic (venous) sinuses in the red pulp, are genuine functional members of the mononuclear phagocytic system, actively filtering blood and phagocytosing aged or damaged red blood cells and other debris as it passes through the splenic sinusoids. This distinguishes them from reticular epithelial cells (structural, non-phagocytic support cells of the thymus), activated B-lymphocytes (antibody-producing cells of the adaptive immune lineage, not the phagocytic lineage), and Merkel's cells (specialised touch-sensing mechanoreceptor cells of the skin, functionally unrelated to phagocytosis).

distractorNotes.A: Reticular epithelial cells provide the structural framework of the thymus (and form the blood-thymic barrier) but are not phagocytic cells themselves.
distractorNotes.B: Activated B-lymphocytes function in antibody production and antigen presentation, part of the adaptive immune lymphocyte lineage, not the phagocytic system.
distractorNotes.D: Merkel's cells are specialised mechanoreceptor cells in the skin responsible for touch sensation, entirely unrelated to phagocytosis.

questions.stem: Which disease increase lung compliance: ‏ظ‎ ‎a- Emphysema
questions.subject: Anatomy

editorialExplanation.explanation: Emphysema destroys alveolar walls and the elastin fibres within them, which reduces the lung's elastic recoil and makes it abnormally easy to inflate -- that is, it increases lung compliance, producing the classic 'floppy lung' of emphysema that also makes exhalation difficult because the lung no longer recoils effectively to push air out. This is the textbook exception among lung diseases, most of which instead reduce compliance by stiffening the lung with fibrous or inflammatory tissue or by filling airspaces with fluid. The exam takeaway is to pair emphysema specifically with INCREASED compliance (destructive, floppy lung), while fibrosis, congestion, and oedema all DECREASE compliance (restrictive, stiff lung) by different mechanisms.

distractorNotes.B: Lung fibrosis stiffens the lung with excess collagenous tissue, decreasing compliance, the opposite effect from emphysema.
distractorNotes.C: Lung congestion (vascular engorgement) stiffens the lung by filling it with excess blood/fluid, decreasing compliance.
distractorNotes.D: Pulmonary oedema fills the interstitium and alveoli with fluid, stiffening the lung and decreasing compliance, the opposite of the increase this question asks about.

questions.stem: Which disorder decreases the chest compliance:
questions.subject: Anatomy

editorialExplanation.explanation: Scoliosis, rib fractures, and paralysis of the respiratory muscles are all classically grouped together as causes of a restrictive breathing pattern with reduced effective chest wall compliance in clinical respiratory physiology teaching: scoliosis and rib fractures mechanically stiffen and deform the thoracic cage directly, while paralysis prevents the normal active expansion that keeps the chest wall operating over its most compliant range, functionally behaving as reduced compliance even though the passive tissue properties themselves are less directly affected. This grouped, 'restrictive disorder' framing is the standard way exam banks test the broader clinical concept of decreased chest wall compliance, rather than isolating each disorder's precise biophysical mechanism. The takeaway is to recognise this category of restrictive chest wall/neuromuscular disorders as a set, contrasted with obstructive lung diseases (like emphysema) that instead increase compliance.

distractorNotes.A: Scoliosis alone genuinely reduces chest wall compliance by structurally deforming the thoracic cage, but it is not the sole correct answer since the other two disorders are also classically included.
distractorNotes.B: Rib fractures alone genuinely reduce effective chest wall compliance (via pain-limited splinting or altered mechanics), but again not the sole correct answer given the grouped framing of this question.
distractorNotes.C: Paralysis of the respiratory muscles alone is classically grouped with the other two disorders as a cause of a restrictive breathing pattern, but again not the sole correct answer here.

questions.stem: Which ef the following are muscles of inspiration?
questions.subject: Anatomy

editorialExplanation.explanation: The diaphragm and the external intercostal muscles are the principal muscles of inspiration: diaphragmatic contraction flattens its dome to increase the vertical dimension of the thoracic cavity, while external intercostal contraction elevates the ribs to increase the anteroposterior and transverse dimensions. Both act to expand thoracic volume and thereby drop intrapleural (and alveolar) pressure below atmospheric, drawing air in -- the defining mechanical requirement of any inspiratory muscle. The takeaway is to pair the diaphragm consistently with the external (not internal) intercostals as the resting-inspiration team, reserving internal intercostals and abdominal muscles for expiration.

distractorNotes.A: Abdominal muscles are expiratory (they raise intra-abdominal pressure to push the diaphragm up), not inspiratory.
distractorNotes.B: Abdominal muscles are expiratory, so pairing them with the diaphragm mixes an inspiratory muscle with an expiratory one.
distractorNotes.D: Internal intercostals depress the ribs and are recruited for forced expiration, the functional opposite of the external intercostals needed for inspiration.

editorialExplanation.explanation: Veins and venules are termed 'capacitance vessels' because their high compliance and large aggregate volume allow them to hold the majority of the body's total circulating blood volume (roughly 60-70%) at any given time, functioning as a low-pressure reservoir that can expand or contract to buffer changes in blood volume and adjust venous return. This is functionally distinct from arteries and arterioles, which are instead termed 'resistance vessels' (or, for large arteries, 'conductance/windkessel vessels'), built to withstand and regulate pressure rather than to store blood volume. The exam takeaway is to pair the term 'capacitance vessel' specifically with veins, holding the largest blood volume share of any vascular compartment.

distractorNotes.A: Arteries hold a comparatively modest share of total blood volume and are termed conductance (or, for arterioles, resistance) vessels, not capacitance vessels.
distractorNotes.C: Capillaries hold only about 5% of total blood volume, the smallest major compartment, and function for exchange rather than volume storage.
distractorNotes.D: Arterioles are termed 'resistance vessels', the primary site of vascular resistance regulation, not capacitance vessels for blood volume storage.

editorialExplanation.explanation: This is a duplicate of the sibling inspiration-muscles question, with the identical correct pairing: the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles are the muscles of (quiet) inspiration, expanding the thorax in its vertical and anteroposterior/transverse dimensions respectively. Internal intercostals and abdominal wall muscles instead belong to the expiratory group, active mainly during forced expiration, so any option pairing them with the diaphragm as 'inspiratory' is incorrect. The consistent exam rule is: external intercostals and diaphragm = inspiration; internal intercostals and abdominal muscles = (forced) expiration.

distractorNotes.A: Abdominal muscles are expiratory, not inspiratory, muscles.
distractorNotes.B: Pairing the diaphragm with abdominal muscles mixes an inspiratory muscle with an expiratory one.
distractorNotes.D: Internal intercostals are expiratory muscles, the functional opposite of what quiet inspiration requires.

questions.stem: Which of the following ceils produce surfactant in lung alveoli?
questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: Type II alveolar cells (pneumocytes) are the dedicated surfactant-producing cells of the alveolar epithelium, synthesising and packaging surfactant phospholipids and proteins within characteristic multilamellar bodies before secreting the mature surfactant onto the alveolar surface, where it reduces surface tension and prevents alveolar collapse. This is distinct from Type I pneumocytes, which are purely structural, thin gas-exchange cells with no secretory function, and from endothelial and goblet cells, which are unrelated to surfactant production altogether.

distractorNotes.A: Endothelial cells form the capillary wall component of the blood-air barrier and have no role in surfactant production.
distractorNotes.B: Goblet cells secrete mucus in the conducting airways (trachea, bronchi), an entirely different secretion from surfactant, and are not found in the alveoli at all.
distractorNotes.C: Type I alveolar cells are thin, purely structural cells adapted for gas exchange; they do not produce surfactant, which is instead a Type II pneumocyte function.

questions.stem: Which of the following conditions would lixely increase the preload?
questions.subject: Physiology

editorialExplanation.explanation: Fluid infusion directly increases circulating blood volume, which raises venous return and ventricular end-diastolic filling -- the direct definition of increased preload. This contrasts with essential hypertension, whose primary haemodynamic effect is increased AFTERLOAD (the pressure the heart must pump against), not preload; hypoalbuminaemia-induced oedema, which shifts fluid OUT of the vasculature into tissues, tending to reduce (not increase) effective circulating volume and preload; and venous thrombosis, which obstructs venous return from the affected area, reducing (not increasing) preload.

distractorNotes.B: Essential hypertension primarily increases afterload (the resistance the heart pumps against), not preload directly.
distractorNotes.C: Hypoalbuminaemia-induced oedema results from fluid shifting out of the vasculature into the interstitium, reducing rather than increasing effective circulating blood volume and preload.
distractorNotes.D: Venous thrombosis obstructs venous return from the affected territory, reducing rather than increasing preload to the heart.

questions.stem: Which of the following decreases the myocardial contractility?

options.C: An increase in end diastolic volume
options.D: An increase in parasympathetic nervous system activity

questions.subject: Physiology

editorialExplanation.explanation: Increased parasympathetic (vagal) activity, acting through muscarinic receptors, inhibits adenylyl cyclase and reduces cAMP/PKA activity, producing a genuine negative inotropic effect that decreases myocardial contractility -- most prominently in the atria, though with some effect on ventricular tissue as well. This contrasts with catecholamines (which increase contractility via beta-adrenergic stimulation), increased heart rate (which, via the force-frequency relationship, tends to modestly increase rather than decrease contractility in most physiological ranges), and increased end-diastolic volume (which affects stroke volume via the separate, preload-dependent Frank-Starling mechanism, without directly changing the heart's intrinsic contractility).

distractorNotes.A: Catecholamines increase, rather than decrease, myocardial contractility via beta-adrenergic stimulation.
distractorNotes.B: An increase in heart rate, via the force-frequency (Bowditch/Treppe) relationship, tends to modestly increase, not decrease, contractility across most physiological rate ranges.
distractorNotes.C: An increase in end-diastolic volume affects stroke volume through the Frank-Starling (preload) mechanism, a distinct concept from intrinsic contractility, which it does not directly decrease.

questions.stem: Which of the following describes the pulse pressure?

options.A: It’s determined by the stroke volume ١
options.B: It's decreased when arterial resistance decreases
options.C: It’s the highest pressure measured in the arteries
options.D: It’s the lowest pressure measured in the arteries

questions.subject: Anatomy

editorialExplanation.explanation: Pulse pressure, the difference between systolic and diastolic arterial pressure, is directly determined by stroke volume (for a given arterial compliance): a larger stroke volume ejects more blood into the arterial tree per beat, producing a larger swing in pressure between systole and diastole. This relationship is why conditions that increase stroke volume without proportionally increasing arterial compliance (such as aortic regurgitation, or the increased stroke volume of exercise) characteristically widen the pulse pressure. The exam takeaway is to keep pulse pressure's two main determinants straight -- stroke volume (increases pulse pressure) and arterial compliance/stiffness (decreased compliance also increases pulse pressure, as in aging arteriosclerosis) -- rather than confusing it with either systolic or diastolic pressure individually.

distractorNotes.B: Pulse pressure is most directly governed by stroke volume and arterial compliance; peripheral arterial resistance primarily determines mean arterial pressure rather than being the main driver of pulse pressure changes.
distractorNotes.C: The highest pressure measured in the arteries is the systolic pressure, not the pulse pressure, which is instead the difference between systolic and diastolic pressure.
distractorNotes.D: The lowest pressure measured in the arteries is the diastolic pressure, not the pulse pressure.

questions.stem: Which of the following discharge spontaneously during quiet breathing? ‏ا‎ ‎a- Stretch receptors ‏ا 18 ا‎
Which of the following discharge spontaneously during quist breathing?
questions.subject: Anatomy

editorialExplanation.explanation: The dorsal respiratory group (DRG) of neurons, located in the medulla's nucleus tractus solitarius, is the intrinsic rhythm generator responsible for the basic automatic cycle of quiet breathing, spontaneously discharging in a repeating inspiratory pattern without needing an external trigger. Motor neurons driving the respiratory muscles and stretch receptors in the lung both fire only in response to input (the DRG's descending drive, or lung inflation, respectively) rather than generating activity on their own. The exam takeaway is that the DRG is the autonomous 'pacemaker' of quiet breathing, while the ventral respiratory group remains largely silent at rest and is recruited mainly for forced breathing (active expiration, exercise).

distractorNotes.A: Stretch receptors in the lung fire in response to lung inflation (a stimulus), not spontaneously on their own.
distractorNotes.B: Motor neurons to the respiratory muscles fire only when driven by descending input from the medullary respiratory centres; they do not generate spontaneous rhythmic activity themselves.
distractorNotes.D: The ventral respiratory group is largely inactive during quiet breathing and is recruited mainly during forced breathing, particularly active expiration.

questions.stem: Which of the following events of cardiac myocyte action potential is correctly described? . : : 1

options.A: Phase [0] shows increased K* conductance through inward rectifying
options.B: In phase [2] the Ca?" influx through T- type channels is balanced by the
options.C: During phase [0] fast sodium channels are inactivated
options.D: During phase [3] delayed rectifier Ky channels are maximally activated

questions.subject: Anatomy

editorialExplanation.explanation: Phase 3 of the cardiac myocyte action potential is the repolarisation phase, driven by the delayed rectifier potassium channels (IKr and IKs) reaching their maximal activation and conductance, allowing potassium efflux to return the membrane potential back toward its resting level. This is the correct, standard description of phase 3's underlying ionic mechanism, distinct from the other phases: phase 0's rapid upstroke depends on fast sodium channel activation (opening, not inactivation), and phase 2's plateau depends mainly on L-type (not T-type) calcium channel influx balanced against a slower, delayed potassium efflux. The exam takeaway is to fix each phase's dominant current precisely: phase 0 = fast Na+ in; phase 1 = transient K+ out; phase 2 = L-type Ca2+ in balanced by K+ out; phase 3 = delayed rectifier K+ out (dominant); phase 4 = resting/pacemaker currents.

distractorNotes.A: Phase 0 is driven by a rapid increase in fast sodium (not potassium) conductance through voltage-gated Na+ channels, producing the steep upstroke.
distractorNotes.B: The plateau phase's calcium influx is carried mainly by L-type calcium channels, not T-type channels, which instead contribute more to pacemaker cell depolarisation.
distractorNotes.C: During phase 0, fast sodium channels are ACTIVATED (open), not inactivated -- inactivation occurs shortly afterward, ending the sodium current and contributing to phase 1.

questions.stem: Which of the following happens during atrial systole of the cardiac cycle?
variants: [EOY 104 Final (198 1st) (1).pdf p14 #11] Which of the following happens during atrial systole of the cardiac cycle? :: A) The first heart sound occurs B) Over 70 % of ventricular filling occurs C) The A-V valves are closed
questions.subject: Physiology

editorialExplanation.explanation: During atrial systole, which occurs entirely within ventricular diastole before ventricular systole begins, the aortic (and pulmonary) semilunar valve remains closed throughout, since ventricular pressure has not yet risen to challenge it. This is in contrast to the AV valves, which are OPEN during atrial systole (allowing the final 'atrial kick' of blood into the ventricles), and the fact that the majority of ventricular filling (roughly 70-80%) actually occurs passively during the earlier rapid filling phase, before atrial systole even begins, with atrial systole itself typically contributing only the remaining 20-30% in a healthy resting heart. The first heart sound, caused by AV valve closure, occurs only after atrial systole ends, at the very start of ventricular systole.

distractorNotes.A: The first heart sound occurs at the start of ventricular systole (AV valve closure), after atrial systole has already ended, not during atrial systole itself.
distractorNotes.B: The majority (roughly 70-80%) of ventricular filling occurs passively during the earlier rapid filling phase of diastole, not specifically during atrial systole, which contributes only the remaining smaller fraction.
distractorNotes.C: The AV valves are OPEN during atrial systole, allowing the atrial kick to push blood into the ventricles -- the opposite of closed.

Which of the following has the slowest rhythmicity in the automatic cardiac tissue?
questions.subject: Anatomy

editorialExplanation.explanation: Among the heart's automatic (autorhythmic) tissues, intrinsic firing rate decreases progressively down the conduction system: the SA node fires fastest (roughly 60-100/min), the AV node next (roughly 40-60/min), and the distal Purkinje/ventricular conduction tissue slowest (roughly 15-40/min), which is why the SA node normally dominates and suppresses the slower latent pacemakers. The Purkinje system's slow intrinsic rate is precisely why it only takes over as a last-resort 'ventricular escape' rhythm if both the SA and AV nodes fail. The takeaway hierarchy to memorise is SA node faster than AV node faster than Purkinje/ventricular tissue, in both conduction velocity and intrinsic rhythmicity.

distractorNotes.A: The SA node has the fastest intrinsic rhythmicity of the automatic tissues, which is why it is the normal pacemaker.
distractorNotes.B: The AV node's intrinsic rate is slower than the SA node's but faster than the distal Purkinje/ventricular tissue's.
distractorNotes.C: The bundle of His is functionally grouped with the Purkinje conduction pathway and shares its slow intrinsic rate range, but the ultimate slowest, most distal automaticity is conventionally attributed to the Purkinje fibres themselves.

questions.stem: Which of the following is associated with a decrease in cardiac output?
variants: [EOM 196 104 2023 No answers  (1).pdf p8 #59] Which of the following is associated with a decrease in cardiac output? :: A) Increased blood volume B) Increased end diastolic volume D) increased myocardial contractility

[DPT BOOK Physio MCQ [104][2023].pdf p7 #26] Which of the following is associated with a decrease in cardiac output? :: A) Increased blood volume B) Increased end diastolic volume C) Venous obstruction D) increased myocardial contractility
questions.subject: Physiology

editorialExplanation.explanation: Venous obstruction impedes the return of blood to the heart, reducing ventricular preload (end-diastolic filling) -- and per the Frank-Starling mechanism, reduced preload directly decreases stroke volume and therefore cardiac output. This is the opposite effect from increased blood volume, increased end-diastolic volume, or increased myocardial contractility, all of which enhance either preload or the heart's pumping efficiency and therefore tend to INCREASE, not decrease, cardiac output.

distractorNotes.A: Increased blood volume typically raises venous return and preload, tending to increase (not decrease) cardiac output via the Frank-Starling mechanism.
distractorNotes.B: Increased end-diastolic volume (preload) directly increases stroke volume via the Frank-Starling mechanism, increasing (not decreasing) cardiac output.
distractorNotes.D: Increased myocardial contractility directly increases stroke volume and cardiac output, the opposite of a decrease.

questions.stem: which of the following is characteristic about the conducting system of the heart:

options.A: Impulses are conducted from the right atrium to the left atrium by the
options.B: The sinoatrial node has an intrinsic rhythmic rate of 40-60 per minute
options.C: The atrioventricular node is the natural pacemaker
options.D: The Purkinje fibers have an intrinsic rhythmic rate of 15-40 per minute

questions.subject: Anatomy

editorialExplanation.explanation: The Purkinje fibres, as the most distal part of the specialised conduction system, have the slowest intrinsic firing rate of the automatic tissues, conventionally cited as about 15-40 beats per minute, which matches option D exactly. This low intrinsic rate is why the Purkinje system never normally sets the heart rate -- it is overridden ('overdrive suppressed') by the faster SA node -- and only emerges as a slow ventricular escape rhythm if higher pacemakers fail. The takeaway is to keep the numeric intrinsic-rate hierarchy straight: SA node ~60-100/min, AV node ~40-60/min, Purkinje ~15-40/min.

distractorNotes.A: Interatrial conduction (right to left atrium) is carried mainly by Bachmann's bundle, a specific named pathway, a detail the option as extracted leaves incomplete rather than clearly true.
distractorNotes.B: 40-60/min is the AV node's approximate intrinsic rate, not the SA node's; the SA node's intrinsic rate is faster, around 60-100/min.
distractorNotes.C: The SA node, not the AV node, is the heart's natural (dominant) pacemaker under normal conditions.

questions.stem: Which of the following is considered a "Positive inotropic mechanism"?

options.B: Activation of Na+-K+ ATPase in sarcolemma
options.C: Activation of muscarinic (M2) receptors and decreased cAMP production
options.D: Activation of protein kinase A leading to increase Ca in the cytoplasm

variants: [DPT BOOK Physio MCQ [104][2023].pdf p3 #3] Which of the following is considered a “Positive inotropic mechanism”? :: A) Ischemia of cardiac muscle B) Inhibition of CAMP production C) Inhibition of Na*-K* pump D) Activation of muscarinic (M2) receptors
questions.subject: Physiology

editorialExplanation.explanation: Activation of protein kinase A, downstream of beta-adrenergic receptor stimulation and increased cAMP, phosphorylates key calcium-handling proteins (L-type calcium channels, phospholamban, troponin I) to increase the amount of calcium available in the cytoplasm during systole, producing the classic positive inotropic pathway underlying sympathetically-enhanced cardiac contractility. This contrasts with cardiac ischemia (which impairs, rather than enhances, contractility), activation of the Na+-K+ ATPase (which would tend to favour calcium extrusion via the Na+-Ca2+ exchanger, reducing rather than increasing cytoplasmic calcium), and muscarinic (M2) receptor activation with decreased cAMP (the classic NEGATIVE, parasympathetic inotropic pathway, the functional opposite of what a positive inotropic mechanism requires).

distractorNotes.A: Cardiac ischemia impairs ATP-dependent calcium handling and REDUCES contractility, a negative, not positive, inotropic influence.
distractorNotes.B: Activating the Na+-K+ ATPase lowers intracellular Na+, which favours the Na+-Ca2+ exchanger extruding more calcium from the cell, tending to REDUCE rather than increase cytoplasmic calcium and contractility.
distractorNotes.C: Muscarinic (M2) receptor activation with decreased cAMP is the classic negative (parasympathetic) inotropic pathway, the functional opposite of a positive inotropic mechanism.

questions.stem: Which of the following is correct?

options.A: The heart receives most of its blood supply during diastole
options.B: Coronary circulation is mainly under neural control
options.C: During systole the % decrease in subendocardial blood flow is greater than the % decrease in
options.E: A&C are correct

questions.subject: Physiology

editorialExplanation.explanation: The heart genuinely receives the majority of its coronary blood supply during diastole, since ventricular contraction during systole compresses the intramural coronary vessels (especially in the left ventricle), impeding flow until the muscle relaxes. During systole, the subendocardial layer -- the innermost, most heavily compressed layer of myocardium -- experiences a proportionally greater percentage reduction in blood flow than the more protected subepicardial layer, making the subendocardium especially vulnerable to ischemia under conditions of increased demand or reduced perfusion pressure. Coronary circulation, in contrast to statement B, is regulated predominantly by local metabolic factors (matching flow tightly to myocardial oxygen demand) rather than by neural control, making the combination of statements A and C the correct comprehensive answer.

distractorNotes.B: Coronary circulation is regulated predominantly by LOCAL METABOLIC factors (adenosine, hypoxia, CO2, and other vasoactive metabolites) matching flow to myocardial oxygen demand, not primarily by neural control.
distractorNotes.C: Statement C alone is true, but the combined answer 'A and C' is more complete than either A or C individually, since both are genuinely correct.
distractorNotes.D: Since statement B is false, the combination 'B and C' cannot be the correct comprehensive answer.

questions.stem: Which of the following is correct as regards excitation-contraction coupling of cardiac myocyte?

options.A: Following membrane depolarization, the large amount of cytoplasmic ©“ is due to calcium- induced calcium release.
options.B: Membrane depolarization will lead to opening of ryanodine-sensitive calcium release channel in the sarcolemma and T-tubules.
options.C: Na’-Ca™ exchanger located at the membrane of terminal cisternae actively reuptakes Ca** back to the sarco-endoplasmic reticulum.

questions.subject: Physiology

editorialExplanation.explanation: Cardiac excitation-contraction coupling is defined by calcium-induced calcium release (CICR): a relatively small amount of calcium entering through L-type calcium channels in the sarcolemma/T-tubules during membrane depolarization triggers ryanodine receptors on the sarcoplasmic reticulum to release a much larger quantity of stored calcium into the cytoplasm, amplifying the signal to drive contraction. This is a defining, correct mechanistic description, in contrast to misattributing the ryanodine receptors' location to the sarcolemma/T-tubules (they are actually on the SR membrane) or misattributing the Na+-Ca2+ exchanger's location and function (it sits on the sarcolemma and extrudes calcium out of the cell, rather than being located on the terminal cisternae and reuptaking calcium into the SR, which is instead SERCA's distinct role).

distractorNotes.B: The ryanodine-sensitive calcium release channels are located on the sarcoplasmic reticulum membrane, not in the sarcolemma or T-tubules, which instead house the L-type calcium channels (dihydropyridine receptors) that trigger CICR.
distractorNotes.C: The Na+-Ca2+ exchanger is located on the sarcolemma (plasma membrane), not the terminal cisternae of the SR, and its function is to extrude calcium OUT of the cell, not to reuptake it back into the SR -- that reuptake role belongs to SERCA, a distinct pump on the SR membrane.

Which of the following is NOT a component of the respiratory membrane? sti(‘S;SSS™~™~™~™”C™

options.A: Plasma membrane of the alveolar cell
options.B: Plasma membrane of the capillary endothelial cell
options.C: Fused basal laminae of the alveolar and the capillary endothelial cell
options.D: Plasma membrane of red blood corpuscle

questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: The respiratory membrane (blood-air barrier) is built from the alveolar epithelial cell's plasma membrane and cytoplasm, the fused basal laminae shared between the alveolar epithelium and the capillary endothelium, and the capillary endothelial cell's own plasma membrane and cytoplasm -- together forming the thin diffusion barrier gases must cross. The red blood corpuscle, while it is what carries the oxygen and carbon dioxide being exchanged across this barrier, is not itself a structural layer of the membrane; it is the cargo flowing through the capillary lumen on one side of the barrier, not part of the barrier's own construction. The exam takeaway is to picture the respiratory membrane as the layered tissue barrier itself (epithelium, fused basal laminae, endothelium), distinct from the blood cells that merely pass through the capillary adjacent to it.

distractorNotes.A: The alveolar epithelial cell's plasma membrane is a genuine structural component of the respiratory membrane.
distractorNotes.B: The capillary endothelial cell's plasma membrane is a genuine structural component of the respiratory membrane.
distractorNotes.C: The fused basal laminae of the alveolar epithelium and capillary endothelium form a genuine structural layer of the respiratory membrane, helping minimise its overall thickness.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a vasodilator metabolite?
questions.subject: Physiology

editorialExplanation.explanation: Endothelin-1 is one of the most potent VASOCONSTRICTOR substances known, produced by vascular endothelial cells and acting on smooth muscle ETA receptors to raise vascular tone -- the functional opposite of a vasodilator metabolite. This contrasts with adenosine, potassium ions, and hydrogen ions, all of which are genuine local vasodilator metabolites released during increased tissue metabolic activity (from ATP breakdown, action potential-related K+ efflux, and anaerobic/aerobic acid production respectively), helping locally match blood flow to the tissue's metabolic demand through metabolic (active) hyperaemia.

distractorNotes.A: Adenosine, released as a breakdown product of ATP during increased metabolic activity, is a genuine, well-established local vasodilator metabolite.
distractorNotes.B: Potassium ions, released during repeated action potentials in active tissue, are a genuine local vasodilator metabolite contributing to metabolic hyperaemia.
distractorNotes.C: Hydrogen ions (from lactic acid or CO2-derived carbonic acid produced during increased metabolism) are a genuine local vasodilator metabolite.

questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: The aorta's tunica intima is not particularly thick -- like most vessels, it consists of just a thin endothelial layer with a modest underlying subendothelial layer -- and its internal elastic lamina is notably NOT well distinguished, since it blends indistinguishably with the many other elastic laminae filling the media, rather than being especially prominent. Both parts of this option are therefore false, making it the correct answer to a 'NOT true' question. By contrast, the aorta genuinely does have a thick tunica media (its most defining structural feature) built from 40 to 70 concentric fenestrated elastic laminae, both of which are well-established, correct facts about this vessel.

distractorNotes.C: The aorta's tunica media is genuinely thick, its most defining structural feature as a large elastic artery.
distractorNotes.D: The aorta's tunica media genuinely contains numerous fenestrated elastic laminae (40-70), the hallmark histological feature of elastic arteries.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the normal order (arrangement) of cardiac cycle phases?

options.A: Rapid filling phase, Reduced ejection phase, Atrial systole, Isovolumetric relaxation phase
options.B: Rapid filling phase, Reduced filling phase, Atrial systole, Isovolumetric contraction phase
options.C: Rapid filling phase, Isovolumetric relaxation phase, Rapid ejection phase, Atrial systole
options.D: Rapid filling phase, Reduced ejection phase, Rapid ejection phase, Isovolumetric contraction phase

questions.subject: Physiology

editorialExplanation.explanation: The correct sequential order of the cardiac cycle's diastolic-to-systolic transition is: rapid filling phase, followed by the reduced filling phase (diastasis), followed by atrial systole, followed by isovolumetric contraction as ventricular systole begins -- exactly the order given in this option. This sequence correctly reflects the physiology: after the initial burst of passive rapid filling and the slower diastasis phase, the atria contract to top off ventricular filling just before the ventricles begin their own isovolumetric contraction, building pressure with all valves closed before ejection can begin.

distractorNotes.A: This sequence incorrectly places reduced ejection (a systolic phase) before atrial systole, and isovolumetric relaxation (which should precede rapid filling) after atrial systole, scrambling the correct order.
distractorNotes.C: This sequence incorrectly places isovolumetric relaxation after rapid filling (it should precede it) and puts rapid ejection and atrial systole in the wrong relative order.
distractorNotes.D: This sequence incorrectly places reduced ejection before rapid ejection (rapid ejection should come first) and puts isovolumetric contraction after both ejection phases instead of before them.

D) Patient with Turner syndrome has one Barr body in her cells
questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: In neutrophils of female individuals, a small drumstick-shaped nuclear appendage -- a classic, distinct manifestation of the Barr body -- can be seen projecting from the nuclear lobes in roughly 3 to 5% of neutrophils examined on a peripheral blood smear, a specific and well-established laboratory finding historically used to help confirm genetic sex or detect X chromosome abnormalities. This differs from the more familiar buccal smear method, where the Barr body appears as a distinct chromatin mass along the inner nuclear envelope, but is not present in literally every single cell examined. The exam takeaway is to remember this specific 3-5% neutrophil 'drumstick' figure as a distinguishing, frequently tested Barr body fact.

distractorNotes.A: The Barr body is present only in cells with more than one X chromosome (i.e., normal female or similar cells), and even then is not visible with equal clarity in literally all cells at all times -- 'all buccal epithelial cells' overstates this.
distractorNotes.C: The number of Barr bodies equals the number of X chromosomes MINUS ONE, not the number of X chromosomes itself.
distractorNotes.D: A Turner syndrome patient (45,X) has only a single X chromosome and therefore shows ZERO Barr bodies, not one.

questions.stem: Which of the following phases shows opening of delayed rectifying K+ channels and increased K+ conductance?
questions.subject: Physiology

editorialExplanation.explanation: Phase 3, the main repolarization phase of the cardiac action potential, is driven by the opening of delayed rectifier potassium channels (IKr and IKs), whose increased K+ conductance allows potassium to efflux and return the membrane potential back toward its resting level. This is distinct from phase 0 (fast Na+ influx, upstroke), phase 2 (balanced Ca2+ influx and K+ efflux, plateau), and phase 4 (funny current and declining K+ conductance, pacemaker depolarization in nodal tissue).

distractorNotes.A: Phase 0 is driven by fast sodium channel opening (Na+ influx), not delayed rectifier K+ channels.
distractorNotes.B: Phase 2 (plateau) reflects a balance between calcium influx and some potassium efflux, but the delayed rectifier K+ channels' full opening and dominance is the defining feature of phase 3, not phase 2.
distractorNotes.D: Phase 4 in pacemaker cells is characterised by a DECREASE in K+ conductance (as delayed rectifier channels close) combined with the funny current, the opposite of delayed rectifier channels opening.

questions.stem: Which of the following phases shows the opening of Na+ funny channels?
questions.subject: Physiology

editorialExplanation.explanation: Phase 4, the slow diastolic (pacemaker) depolarization unique to nodal tissue, is when the 'funny' current (If) channels open, carrying a mixed but significantly Na+-mediated inward current that helps drive the membrane potential slowly toward threshold. This is distinct from phase 0 (fast Na+ channels, not funny channels, driving the rapid upstroke), phase 2 (calcium channels dominating the plateau), and phase 3 (potassium channels dominating repolarization).

distractorNotes.A: Phase 0's rapid upstroke is driven by fast voltage-gated sodium channels, a different channel type from the funny (If) channels.
distractorNotes.B: Phase 2 (plateau) is dominated by calcium channel activity, not funny channels.
distractorNotes.C: Phase 3 (repolarization) is dominated by potassium channel activity (delayed rectifiers), not funny channels.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements regarding the phrenic nerves is | true?

options.A: In the superior mediastinum, the left phrenic nerve is crossed by the left
options.B: They pass posterior to roots of lungs
options.C: They share in the formation the esophageal plexus of nerves
options.D: They contain only somatic motor nerve fibers,
options.E: The right phrenic nervesupplies sensory fibers to the peritoneum covering

questions.subject: Anatomy

editorialExplanation.explanation: The phrenic nerve is a mixed nerve, and its sensory component famously extends beyond the diaphragm itself to the peritoneum covering the diaphragm's central part on its abdominal (inferior) surface -- this is the anatomical basis for the well-known clinical phenomenon of referred shoulder-tip pain when the diaphragm or adjacent peritoneum is irritated (e.g. by blood, bile, or gas after laparoscopic surgery), since the phrenic nerve's C3-C5 dermatomal representation is shared with the shoulder region. This sensory territory extending onto the peritoneal surface, rather than being purely a motor nerve to the diaphragm muscle, is precisely what makes this statement true and clinically important. The takeaway is to remember the phrenic nerve as a genuinely mixed nerve, carrying somatic motor fibres to the diaphragm plus sensory fibres from the diaphragm's central peritoneal and pleural coverings and the fibrous pericardium.

distractorNotes.B: The phrenic nerves pass ANTERIOR to the roots of the lungs, not posterior -- this anterior/posterior distinction (phrenic anterior, vagus posterior to the lung root) is one of the most frequently tested facts pairing these two nerves.
distractorNotes.C: The oesophageal plexus is formed by the vagus nerves (anterior and posterior vagal trunks), not the phrenic nerves.
distractorNotes.D: The phrenic nerve is a mixed nerve carrying both somatic motor fibres (to the diaphragm) and sensory fibres (from the diaphragm, mediastinal pleura, and pericardium), not purely somatic motor fibres.

questions.subject: Histology

editorialExplanation.explanation: Medium-sized (muscular) arteries are defined by a tunica media dominated by many layers of smooth muscle cells, interspersed with some elastic fibres, which allows active regulation of vascular tone and resistance along the arterial tree. This muscular media is bounded by a well-developed, clearly visible internal elastic lamina (a key identifying feature of this vessel type), and vasa vasorum, where present, are located in the tunica adventitia rather than the intima. The exam takeaway is to fix the muscular artery's signature identity as 'smooth-muscle-rich media with a prominent internal elastic lamina', distinct from the elastic artery's many-elastic-laminae media and the vein's thicker adventitia.

distractorNotes.A: Vasa vasorum, where present in a vessel wall, are located in the tunica adventitia, not the tunica intima.
distractorNotes.C: Medium-sized arteries have a well-developed, prominent internal elastic lamina -- one of their most distinguishing microscopic features -- not an absent one.
distractorNotes.D: It is the tunica media, not the adventitia, that is the thicker, dominant layer in arteries; a thicker adventitia relative to media is instead a defining feature of veins.

questions.stem: Why the Na+ funny channels are called "Hyperpolarization-activated Cyclic Nucleotide-regulated channels"?

options.B: They are regulated by intracellular cAMP
options.C: They can depolarize the pacemaker cell to +30 mV
options.D: Only A and B are correct

questions.subject: Physiology

editorialExplanation.explanation: The funny current channels' full name, 'Hyperpolarization-activated Cyclic Nucleotide-gated' (HCN) channels, directly encodes both of their defining properties: they are activated by hyperpolarization (opening as the membrane potential becomes more negative, unlike most voltage-gated channels, which open with depolarization), and their activity is modulated by intracellular cyclic nucleotides, particularly cAMP (explaining how sympathetic stimulation, via increased cAMP, speeds their activation and increases heart rate, while parasympathetic stimulation, via decreased cAMP, slows them). Both naming components are correct and complementary, making the combined answer the most complete and accurate.

distractorNotes.A: This captures only half of the channel's defining name (the hyperpolarization-activation property) without the cyclic-nucleotide-regulation component.
distractorNotes.B: This captures only half of the channel's defining name (the cyclic nucleotide regulation) without the hyperpolarization-activation component.
distractorNotes.C: The funny current contributes to slow depolarization toward threshold, not depolarizing the cell all the way up to +30 mV -- that overshoot is instead achieved by later, different channels (Ca2+ channels in nodal tissue) during the action potential's upstroke, not by the funny channels' own naming rationale.

questions.subject: Physiology

editorialExplanation.explanation: The sinoatrial node has the fastest intrinsic rate of spontaneous (auto-rhythmic) depolarization of any cardiac tissue -- faster than the AV node, and far faster than the His-Purkinje system -- which is precisely why it always reaches threshold and fires first, triggering each heartbeat before any other latent pacemaker can spontaneously activate ('overdrive suppression'). This intrinsic rate hierarchy, not its anatomical location, autonomic innervation, or specific channel kinetics in isolation, is the fundamental reason the SA node dominates as the heart's normal pacemaker.

distractorNotes.B: Other cardiac tissues also receive autonomic innervation to varying degrees; having both sympathetic and parasympathetic input is not itself the defining reason the SA node functions as the dominant pacemaker.
distractorNotes.C: The SA node's location in the right atrium is an anatomical fact, not the physiological reason its intrinsic rhythm dominates over other pacemaker tissue.
distractorNotes.D: Potassium channel kinetics contribute to the pacemaker potential's mechanism, but the defining reason the SA node dominates as pacemaker is its overall fastest intrinsic firing rate, not this specific channel property in isolation.
